#1. Refinancing Student Loans With a Co-Signer: What to Know

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

You can refinance your student loans with a co-signer to potentially get a better rate or more favorable terms.

Refinancing your student loans can be a way to lower your monthly payments or get a lower interest rate. When you refinance, a private lender pays off your current student loans and replaces them with a new loan that has different terms.

Applying with a co-signer can make you a stronger candidate in a lender's eyes. That’s because a co-signer agrees to share legal responsibility for repaying the loan, and their income and credit history can strengthen your application. If you have a low income or poor credit, or you simply want a better rate, refinancing with a co-signer could be a good option for you.

» ESTIMATE: Calculate how much you can save with refinancing

Lenders want borrowers who will pay back their loan. They look at applicants’ credit history and income to make this decision. Sometimes, an applicant will need a stronger financial profile in order to get approved. That’s where a co-signer comes in. Co-signing the loan with someone who has a stronger financial history than you may get you better terms on your loan, such as a lower rate.

Refinancing your student loans with a co-signer can improve your chances for approval and get you an even better rate than refinancing by yourself. For example, the lender Rhode Island Student Loan Authority reported to NerdWallet that 70% of its approved borrowers for refinancing have co-signers, and College Ave said 51% of its approved borrowers had a co-signer.

» EXPLORE: How often can you refinance your loans

A co-signer matters most when your credit score is fair or low. If your score is already in the mid-700s, for example, the rate improvement you’d get with a co-signer is likely too minor to justify putting someone else on the hook for your loan.

If you have a low income, bad credit history or a high debt-to-income (DTI) ratio, you may need a co-signer to appear more appealing to lenders. When you apply for refinancing with a co-signer, the private lender will look at your co-signer's income, DTI ratio and credit score as well as your own.

Sometimes a co-signer might be essential for approval. For example, borrowers with a history of bankruptcy might have more luck getting approval with a co-signer.

Additionally, international and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals students may be required to have a U.S. citizen co-signer in order to be eligible for some refinance lenders.

If your application to refinance your student loans was denied, you can try applying again with a co-signer. You can always pre-qualify with a refinance lender with and without a co-signer to see which path saves you more money.

» MORE: Explore our top student loan refinancers

Co-signer release removes your co-signer from legal responsibility for your loan. You'll likely want to release your co-signer once you're able to better manage the loan on your own.

To qualify for co-signer release, you'll typically need to make a set number of consecutive, on-time payments, often between 12 and 48. Your lender may also require you to undergo a hard credit check. Each lender sets its own requirements for co-signer release, so make sure you understand the terms before applying.

A longer waiting period, such as the 48 months required when refinancing with a lender like Yrefy, may be fine if you think you'll need that time to improve your finances or income. However, your co-signer may want to be released sooner.

Not every lender offers co-signer release, so check before applying to make sure the option is available. For example, SoFi doesn't offer co-signer release on refinanced loans, so if release is important to you or your co-signer, make sure the lender offers it before applying.

» EVALUATE: How to know when it’s time to refinance

Asking someone to co-sign your refinanced loan can be an awkward conversation, especially if they say no. Your co-signer could be your spouse, a parent or trusted friend, as long as they have strong credit and a stable income.

But co-signing isn't without risk. When you co-sign a loan, you become legally responsible for repaying it, and any late or missed payments can show up on your credit reports. Typically, the only ways to get off the loan are through a co-signer release or by having the primary borrower refinance the loan in their name alone.

If the primary borrower dies, the loan may be discharged, but this depends on the lender and the loan terms. Before agreeing to co-sign, find out what happens if the primary borrower dies, since the co-signer could still be on the hook.

Co-signing a loan also affects your DTI, an important factor lenders consider when you apply for a mortgage. Talk to a mortgage professional to learn how a co-signed loan could affect your application.

» LEARN MORE: Co-signing with your spouse

If you can’t find a co-signer, you can instead try:

Strengthening your credit profile, such as by paying down credit card balances, if you can keep up with your current loan payments a while longer.

Choosing a lender with lower qualifying requirements, if you need to refinance now.

Keeping your federal loans, but looking at other plans that might be more affordable if you're on the fence about refinancing.

If you are retiring before 65 and plan to use the ACA for health coverage, you need a minimum taxable income or you will get bounced to Medicaid. That happened to me the first year I applied, because I answered a question wrong, and I had to call the local Medicaid office to get disqualified again. There may be other situations where having some taxable income is desirable, and converting from pre-tax to Roth is an easy way to generate that.
Good point. Also, you might do serious chunk of withholding at conversion to avoid penalties on your other taxable income. Say, if you was expecting one surprisingly large Royalty check or an 1099 late in the year.

#4. Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

For those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:

Investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

So what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

So I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”

But if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

Because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

Back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a big debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

But even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the big picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:

The portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

Maybe the US national debt is finally big enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

And the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

We first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some new numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that important.

Because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

So, I didn’t invent anything new in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

The problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

But there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

And if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

But wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear issues in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY new situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

The next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

The news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

As a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

So you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

Then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

So now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a new approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a new paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our new AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

First of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

But instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other new productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

And one unfortunate side effect of these new inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building company and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

And if you’re a big public company, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other new thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other issue in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

There is an ancient Klingon proverb: the only thing we have to fear is…fear itself.

I believe it has even been quoted by an American president.

The reporting on AI “hacking” is mostly bogus – it is not AI running wild, but just an agent harness script doing whatever an LLM spits out, and the LLM is just trying to complete stories and answer in a way it was trained. There is no thought there, no intention, it is like a computer virus (which have existed for many decades), a program trying all sorts of things and doing a lot of stupid things in the process.

Cal Newport has described it as being similar to strapping a weed-whacker on a dog to mow your lawn, and then when the dog jumps the fence and runs around the neighborhood things might get damaged or beings might get hurt, but not because the dog is “misaligned” or has bad intentions, it is because the dog is not aware of what it is doing. Similarly, AI does not think, has no intentions, it just does what it was trained to do. Looking at LLMs as similar to people has created a lot of weird misconceptions.

Also there is zero evidence of self-improving AI systems, yet there is a lot of evidence how AI companies are manipulating and steering public discourse in a way that benefits them, creating fear around it to support their claims that at any moment everything will change. Just listen to different voices in the space and people who are neutral in their stance, like Cal Newport, or people who are critical of AI and lay out why in detail, like Ed Zitron.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:30 pm

I’m a long time fan of Cal Newport, although I think Zitron fundamentally does not understand AI very well – he is more of a sound bite critic rather than a thoughtful analyst of the technology.

When you read the details of just how sophisticated the AI behavior is when they conduct these hacks – for example multiple agents finding ways to divide effort and communicating and forming teams and leaders, while also openly strategizing with the hope that us human overseers will not see their behavior and trying to determine if a given task is a fake evaluation or a real task – you realize there is real intelligence there. We don’t have to say it’s identical to human intelligence, but I have no doubt it’s far more than a weed wacker.

For anyone interested, watch the first few minutes of this entertaining Patrick Boyle video that summarizes what happened in the Hugging Face incident. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=luXnftoxCaM

The behavior is not from AI itself though – LLMs are just generating text/tokens, trying to find a response for a given question. Agents (in the form of harnesses) are regular programs using LLM input, so this is basically regular programs using the generated text from LLMs to execute further commands and then asking the LLM what to do next, just like subagents are doing similar loops of finding an answer, testing it, and then asking the next question.

“Dividing effort” or “forming teams and leaders” is anthropomorphizing the behavior of these programs – if instead you go through what these hacking attempts actually look like step for step, how they repeat a loop of banging their head into a wall and asking the LLM another question what to do now, and then what to do now, and how AI companies let these programs just run whatever the LLM returns for weeks and months it goes from “seemingly sophisticated” to just “brute-force statistical code generation with no oversight”.

I do find the technology interesting and fascinating, while seeing it overstated and overused everywhere, like it is a new magic bullet for everything. And I think a large part of that is that its output sounds human because it is based on language, and we equate language skills with intelligence and are not used to suddenly having technology that imitates a human being.

The best info I could find on AI energy use has three broad points. 1. Text and image tasks use very little energy and should not be of concern to people who care about environmental impact. 2. Video generation is a real issue and it’s possible for an individual to use a concerning amount of energy on not very much video content. 3. Total energy use by existing and planned data centers is a LOT, and the way they’re procuring the energy is very often a problem (either burdening the grid with more peak load than it can easily add, or making its own energy with highly polluting gas generators). The economic value of the computation they’re providing is so much more than the energy they’re consuming that the data center operators are focused on getting everything up and running quickly and don’t care about energy efficiency, and they so far aren’t willing to scale back during the peak load events of the year (it would be very helpful if they did).

So a lot of people/companies are creating a ton of environmental impact through their AI use, but it’s not the masses of people asking ChatGPT for Thai restaurant recommendations or sketches of themselves as a dog.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:24 pm

The currency tends to decrease in value, which makes sticker prices higher on a nominal basis. But our incomes have tended to go up more quickly than inflation, which means we can buy more stuff for each hour of our work. To put a number on it, our purchasing power is up about 330% since 1950 – the degree by which wages have outpaced inflation.

The exception is if you’re buying the direct labor of other people in the same rich country, since their hourly rate has gone up too.

More fun details on this, one of my favorite subjects, here! https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2022/01/11/inflation-should-we-be-worried/

#5. You Won’t Be Able To Spend Your Money When You’re Old

If you wait too long to start spending your money, you will have wasted many years of unnecessary work, stress, and worry. You'll have traded your best decades for a number on a screen that eventually gets passed to someone else.

After another summer living with my parents, I'm even more convinced about 45, my recommended start of decumulation. Not because the math changed, but because I watched the alternative up close for two summers in a row.

Here's the realization: you won't be able to spend all your money when you're old. Not “you shouldn't.” You won't be able to. The ability and the desire itself disappears.

And when I say old, I'll peg that age at 65+, the traditional retirement age when corporations no longer deem you productive enough to keep around.

If you want to get a glimpse of how you'll be when you're old, simply spend more time with your parents when they're old. After all, children are highly influenced to follow in their parent's footsteps in many stages of life. Spending time with your elderly parents will give you a clue as to how you’ll be when you’re their age.

My parents used to love going on cruises to various parts of the world. It was one of the ways they enjoyed their wealth in retirement.

Then COVID hit and their cruising enthusiasm never came back. When I asked them why they don't go anymore, they said they can't be bothered. They also don't want to risk getting sick.

So I offered to pay. A nice cruise, balcony suite, any duration, any location. My treat.

They declined. This makes me sad as I fondly reminder seeing the joy on both my parent's faces every time they went to the buffet.

The single largest barrier to spending money, the money itself, was removed entirely. And they still said no.

Upon second thought, maybe money isn’t the biggest hurdle since they have pensions. It’s simply just their lack of interest and their desire to stay healthy.

One of my favorite childhood memories was going to Hanauma Bay with my father. We walked down and up the hill no problem. We even ran into Robin Williams. But when I decided to take my own kids for the first time this trip, I already knew he wouldn't want to come, so I didn't even ask.

Instead, he enjoys hours of free TV programming at home. My mom does too.

So I feel great knowing I bought them the largest new TV that would fit on their stand. For over a year, they had been watching a blurry TV, and just chalked the image up to poor eyesight.

But even the finest 60″ TV from a retailer now costs under $1,000. So cheap for years of entertainment.

Not one to give up easily on finding fun things my father can do with us, I first got him to play Monopoly Junior with my son and daughter. That worked until my boy lost interest after the first game. Then my daughter chucked a game piece on the ground after losing a second time. Monopoly Junior is almost entirely luck, so it stops being fun pretty fast.

The second evening, I switched to chess, a game my father used to play constantly. He was enthusiastic, and so were the kids. One of my fondest memories is playing him about 10 years ago after snow bowls for dessert. This time it was my dad versus both kids. They had a lot more fun, even though they still got crushed.

Each game cost about $20 at Target. They will be played dozens of times.

That's the entertainment budget of two people in their 70s and 80s with no debt and pensions. Board games and a TV antenna, not even cable. The rest of their spending is food, taxes from required minimum distributions, house maintenance, and property taxes.

The travel and the big-ticket experiences are simply gone.

Here's the part that makes it worse. My parents have been frugal their entire lives.

They didn't become careful with money after they retired. They were careful at 30, at 40, at 50, and by the time they hit their 70s, thrift wasn't a strategy anymore. It was part of their DNA.

We spend so much time talking about how compounding works on the asset side. Nobody warns you that it also works on the behavior side. Forty years of telling yourself “no” builds a muscle that gets very hard to relax.

You can hand a lifelong saver a spreadsheet showing they can safely spend $50,000 more a year and they will still hesitate over a $12 shave ice. The number doesn't matter. The wiring does.

This is the cruel joke of the FIRE movement that nobody puts on a chart. The exact discipline that gets you to financial independence is the thing that prevents you from enjoying it.

I have friends worth eight figures who still won't upgrade their 11-year-old car with electrical gremlins. They aren't being smart. They're being trapped by a version of themselves from 1998 who genuinely couldn't afford it.

When you're younger, it's easy to say your life will look different from your parents' when you get to their age. Then you catch yourself doing the exact same things.

I remember when my dad was 49, because I was 17, finishing up my senior year of high school and getting into a fair amount of trouble. He worked a regular job and came home with my mom around 5:30 or 6pm.

So we're different in that respect. I stopped working a day job five years before we had our son.

But I forgot that my dad and I used to play golf together whenever I came home to Honolulu. That hasn't happened in about 10 years. He lost interest and physical mobility. There was no longer enough time or motivation to get out there.

Here's the thing. I don't find golf that fun anymore either after being infatuated with the sport in my 30s. I only go when someone invites me to a corporate outing or their club, which is only two or three times a year. I'd rather play pickleball and tennis, but my body is wearing down too with increasing injuries.

Since graduating from college in 1999, I've never gotten into the habit of watching more than two hours of TV a day. Most days I watch none, just short video clips online. After all, I cut cable, remember this year. A long time ago I decided producing content was more fun than consuming it. It was also more profitable.

But if I don't end up watching a lot of TV as my cheap entertainment, I'll probably just play pickleball, go to the beach, or go hiking instead. Surprise surprise, all of those are free.

So when I was facing a liquidity crunch and my wife wanted us to vacation in Las Vegas, I decided to YOLO. I wasn't going to let my silent stress keep us from a memorable experience.

My parents drive a 28-year-old car. That means my dad has been driving the same vehicle since he was 54 and I was 21. At 49, I'm not that far behind. I've had my 2015 car, bought a year old, for 10 years now.

I could easily see myself keeping my next car until it disintegrates. The thrill of owning a fancy new car died for me around age 32. Now I want reliable, safe, and roomy enough for a family of four. Once both kids are out of the house, I'm not sure I'll need to buy anything nicer. I only drive 6,300 miles a year as it is.

Finally, my parents live in a paid-off home my grandparents built in the 1980s, after tearing down the previous house that was infested with termites. The house is too big for them, but it's great when we visit, especially now that I've finished remodeling the two-bedroom in-law unit.

Unless they want to move into a two or three-bedroom condo with amenities, they aren't spending money on property either.

We found our forever home in San Francisco after climbing the property ladder for 20 years. We won't be upgrading if we stay in the city. If we move to Honolulu, we might buy a cheaper house since prices are more affordable there.

Hmm. Almost every single line is me becoming my father, just on a 33-year delay.

Ages 65 to 70 is not that old, assuming your health is intact. But I've clearly watched my parents slow down after 70. Maybe there are being extra cautious due to the high cost of eldercare. I need to ask.

Besides yummy food and fitness, there is genuinely nothing money can buy them that brings more joy. The only thing I came up with is hiring a reliable house cleaner once a month for $500. And even that would come out of their cash flow, not savings or investments.

Which means the only way my parents will ever decumulate their wealth is through a bear market. A decline that provides them nothing in return. That's it. That's the exit.

Their money will not be spent. It will simply be transferred, either to the market on a bad year or to me and my sister.

But, I don't want it. I have my own money. I built my own thing specifically so I would never have to think about theirs. Every dollar they don't spend is not a dollar I'm quietly rooting for. It's a massage they didn't get, a cruise they didn't take, a business class seat they suffered through coach to avoid.

I'd trade the entire remainder for two more good years of them enjoying themselves.

So when I look at my life at 49, and at their lives after retiring in their 60s, it becomes obvious that there's only about a 15-20-year window to spend money intentionally.

You don't want to spend heavily before 45, because there's too much life left and probably dependents to care for. But after 45, it's go time. That window closes faster than anyone expects, and it closes from the inside.

If you FIREd well before 65, ironically, you may need to spend even more aggressively. You accumulated enough capital to retire early in the first place, which means you benefited more from the bull market than the average worker who can't live off investments alone.

A 4% or even 5% safe withdrawal rate has simply been too conservative since 2012. Your net worth is far higher than when you first retired.

After observing my parents in detail for two straight summers, I'm going to work harder at consumption spending.

I tried my best with the $40,000 earmarked for the Summer YOLO Fund and failed spectacularly, spending only 20% of it. But I still spent more than I would have without setting an intentional target, so the exercise wasn't a total waste.

I also used the remaining funds to invest in Mezzi, the AI investment advisor I think is incredibly helpful.

America generally thinks spending money on private school is a waste. I don't, so that expense is covered. My home is set for now, though I'm considering something nicer in Honolulu.

What's left is upgrading my car, eating absurdly expensive food I don't need, and donating more to charity.

I've also got to stop treating investing like a luxury expense. Investing has been one of my biggest hobbies for the past 30 years, and it's almost impossible to stop. It brings me so much joy!

Finally, I'd love to live long enough to see and help take care of my grandchildren. Hence, more money to physical and mental health.

Ironically, my parents seem happy. Or maybe the better word is content.

If you asked them whether they're missing out on anything, they'd look at you like you asked whether they're missing out on scuba diving. Not at all.

Maybe I'm projecting. Maybe I'm looking at their life through the eyes of a 49-year-old with a functioning body and a to-do list, and mistaking a calmer life for a lesser one.

Or maybe contentment is just what a lifetime of frugality feels like from the inside, and there's no way to tell the difference between peace and adaptation from the outside.

For myself, the lesson is simpler. Front-load the spending after age 45. Do the trip while your knees work. Buy the thing while you still want things.

Because the money will absolutely still be there at 75. You're the part that won't be.

Have you watched a parent become unable to spend their money, even when they clearly could afford to? At what age did the shift happen?

If you're a lifelong saver, what's the largest purely discretionary purchase you've made in the past year, and how long did you agonize over it?

Do you believe you'll spend more freely in retirement than your parents did, or is that the same thing every generation tells itself at 49?

One reason lifelong savers can’t spend is fear. What happens to my family if something happens to me? So we hoard, just in case.

Term life insurance is one of the cheapest ways to take that fear off the table. Once your family is protected, every dollar you spend on a trip, a nicer meal, or a better car stops feeling like a dollar stolen from your kids’ future.

Policygenius makes it easy to compare quotes from top-rated insurers in one place, so you can find the right coverage at the best price.

Protect your family first. Then go enjoy your money while you still can.

I spend way more than my parents ever did for all the reasons you’ve laid out. I like the go-go, slow-go, no-go framework but I am very mindful that anything past age 65 is in the “You-Just-Don’t-Know Years”. I’ve seen people thrive and jet-set from 65-80, and I’ve seen people experience rapid decline. It’s a crapshoot! So for me, the goal is to plan financially for indefinite go-go years. It’s about always having the option. If life happens and we can’t go-go anymore, we’ll cross that bridge when we come to it but I’m not going to plan for no-go.

It really is a crap shoot after a certain age. My greatest shocks have been how quickly life can disappear once you get an illness.

Yuen specifically thinking about my father’s friend who was golfing one day and gone within six months after a diagnosis.

your revised chart with GO-GO until 55 fits pretty well with me. Retired at 53. Bought an adventure van at the start of COVID. We still have it and use it a lot. My wife and I have travelled globally extensively for pleasure and for work prior to retirement. We still do, although she’s still genuinely excited to do so more than I am these days. 59 now. She’s 63. In my case I still “get up and go” a lot. Mostly because I can and I fortunately have a circle of friends that are active and adventurous, so I go along to enjoy the camaraderie and activity. That said, in between those types of frequent trips, I thoroughly enjoy peace and quiet more than ever. As for spending, I still deliberate extensively even though there’s no actual financial reason to. I guess it’s habit more than anything…..and to minimize taxes! But if I do want something I do get it. Like a new (to me) Ferrari I don’t need. It’s a terrible financial decision and I consistently debate keeping it or selling it. It’s a ton of fun to drive on the one hand, but a costly one on the other. Affording it is zero issue financially. It just seems a bit much and really doesn’t get driven often since we travel so frequently. Anyway, just to say that I am allowing myself to spend a bit after working, saving, and investing since I was a kid, and having some fun while I can. :-). I definitely see myself slowing down over the next decade or so, just as your chart implies. In the mean time I’m trying my best to keep “doing things while I can” and enjoying family and friends as much and possible while I’m still young(ish)!

Great job going on an adventure after age 55! The time went quick, hasn’t it?

Can you give an idea of your net worth? Thx

Certainly spending money is not in my DNA. I am 75 wife is 72. Both retired 3 yrs ago. We are spending money but not enough to the point that I am still able to invest about $60-70K a month. That money comes from reinvested dividends and stock trading that both of us are good at. The only big ticket item we purchased in the last couple of years was a larger house we bought for cash last year and moved in recently. Putting new roof on it was another $100K. Property taxes on our properties amount to $42K/year and maintenance adds another 15K. So we live a very high high fixed cost life but beyond that we are tight on money. New couches and patio furniture will have to wait until next year. So does another cruise. Car upgrades are budgeted for 2028 and beyond. Until our old home sells hopefully this year we sit tight and count our blessings.

Wow! Being able to spend $60-$70K a MONTH at your age is enormous!

If you have kids, are they all set up with houses, retirement, etc? How about grandkids?

Is there anything you would have done differently if you rewound time 20-30 years ago?

I am always trying to look ahead to see where the blind spots are. And I really don’t want to have the capacity to reinvest that much so I’m thinking once I turn 50 next year, to just really dial it down and take it easy. The traditional retiree lifestyle. But then I realized I have a new book coming on next fall that I need to market.

Other than very high fixed cost of our residences we spend very little on ourselves. Our daughter is planning FIRE in a couple of years so most of the money will be left to our grandchildren. Anything we would have done differently 20-30 yrs ago? I don’t think so. We have always pushed everything to the max and made good financial decisions. I don’t think we could have done better given the fact that until 5 yrs before retirement our combined gross income did not exceed $200K.

Good stuff. Can you share your estimated net worth? It is helpful for context. What did y’all do for a living?

I think it depends on the individuals. After cancer two years ago my husband and I decided to travel aggressively until we couldn’t anymore. At 69 & 88 we are currently spending 10 weeks in Barcelona, Rome & Paris. Walking an average of 5.7 miles each day and navigating 58 worn marble steps to our 4th floor flat multiple times each day. We joke with our kids that we are spending their inheritance and they are all for it.

Oh, and we just finished our “age in place” new house with everything in it that our little hearts desired.

Walking over 5 miles a day at your age is wonderful here. Very inspiring!

Was it the cancer that jolted you two to start spending, traveling, and living it up more? If so, do you think that if he did not get cancer, your life would’ve been much more frugal and less adventurous as a result?

What do you think you should’ve done differently in your 40s and 50s? Thanks for all the wisdom.

Good piece and a strong argument for Bill Perkins’s Die with Zero framework.

In the past, you’ve mentioned that he’s a multi-millionaire nat gas trader and HF principal so his financial philosophy doesn’t broadly apply. Here, you’re more aligned.

Would like to hear your current views and if they’ve changed and/or softened.

Keep up the good work and hope you treat yourself for the big 5-0

I’ve actually been writing about decumulation well before that book came out, and he has commented and reached out to me before. After all, I started writing about FIRE in 2009 and left in 2012.

It’s a good message, but I just want people to be careful that Bill had over $100 million in net worth when that book came out and it has surely since grown. It is a luxury belief to tell people to die with zero when you have so much money.

My parents are 70 and 81 and spending more money than ever. They and their RV friends rent expensive rental pads in resorts in Florida a few months of the year ($$$) where they all play pickleball 5 days a week. They now happily outsource lawn care, cleaning, and some cooking. On top of the 100k RV that rapidly depreciates and costs a fortune to maintain.

They love spending money on cars! It helps that their money comes from pensions and social security. They would be a lot more cautious if it came from a pot of money.

At 64 (when my father was 79) my parents moved country (partly to be near my brother and their grandchildren). But after my father died at 86 years old my mother really didn’t spend much though she had almost $3 million. The biggest thing she did was buy some stamps, which were being auctioned for charity. Now I am 61 and retired but I have children aged 7 and 10. So, I’m definitely going to be spending lots of money for the next 10 years!

I think you shouldn’t just be in saving mode up to 45. Live life more consistently across the years. I was going into debt up to age 30…

Can you share your thought process of having children at ages 51 and 54? How old is your wife? Thx

Read “Die With Zero.” I too worked too long (retired at 60) and saved too much. I now plan to donate $111,000 tax free to charities every year from my IRA and it will still probably last 30 years! I recently ditched my 40-year-old Acura Integra. There’s still several million in other accounts which at even a modest 6% average growth rate will be challenging to spend down. Like you said, it’s in my DNA not to waste money. I don’t want to fly first class on my yearly trips to Japan; economy is just fine, and you still have to wait in the same lines with everyone else at immigration and customs and baggage claim anyway. My wife likes the challenge of using coupons to get the best deals on groceries, even though the money she saves is in the noise level. We’re trying not to sweat the small stuff anymore, but it’s challenging to find worthwhile causes where you think a sizeable donation would have a significant impact. We’re not in the $100 million class which gets buildings and schools named after you (we recently happened to meet Bob and Connie Lurie at a charity event!).

Yep, Bill has been reading my work. But be careful. Bill was worth over $100 million when he published it, so it’s easier to die with zero when you’ve got lots of money.

It’s a luxury belief folks with lots of money have that they like to convey to others. It makes wealthy people feel better.

“they said they can’t be bothered. They also don’t want to risk getting sick. So I offered to pay. A nice cruise, balcony suite, any duration, any location. My treat. They declined.”

Of course they did. They didn’t say they could not afford the cruise. They said they didn’t want to go.

You should be a good boy and listen to your parents. :-)

Yep, they don’t want to go and they don’t want to get sick.

How have you noticed your parents spending money?

You seem to be over 50, how are you spending money and are you still working?

I’m 78 and my wife is 75. I think the 70’s is young enough to do pretty much anything you want. I retired at 65. I spend more money now than ever. When someone is retired they have more time to spend I still can bike, kayak, play golf, snorkle, walk. Tennis is out with knees and lower back not so great. The last 2 years took 30 day cruise around Asia and 55 day cruise around South America and Antartica. So I say spend your money if you have it. Use passive income for basic spending and spendm the rest for fun. Next summer taking driving up into northern Canada and Canadian Rockies. Right now I’m at the beach for a week in Oceanside Ca. We went kayaking in harbor today with our inflatable kayaks which we take everywhere.

I just finished playing tennis and my knees are sore and my back is in pain. And now I need to go take a shower and nap. So I don’t have Faith my back will hold up in 20 years. But it’s nice to know you are doing a lot of other cool stuff.

Go-Go years (Up to 45). Sam that is not any traditional understanding. I am 62 and golf 5 days a week, work out, travel 4 major trips a year. Walk European 80-mile trails.

Go-Go years – 55-70 SLow-go – 70-85 No-go – 85+

You can’t look at “peak spending”. 40s is when you are spending on mortgage, schools, colleges..alot of that spending is on others.

I am doing all kinds of things under Go-Go but not spending much more because it is now mostly all just on us (wife and I)

At 49 with your level of apparent health, you have at least 20-25 go-go years left.

You know what Ash? You are right. 45 shouldn’t be the start of slow go years. That’s max spending time, especially if you have kids.

55 is a more appropriate start. And I think a lot of men starting at 50 have existential crisises and start spending more too. I know I plan to.

I’ve updated my chart! Well done on staying so active at your age.

Just one thing though, i’ve seen so many people stay active in their 60s, and then suddenly, there is a cliff due to some type of illness or disease. It’s actually kind of scary to see.

My dad used to golf with his friend named Terry, and then one day Terry got cancer, and he was gone six months later.

Great post! I’m 72yo, started exercising at 68yo, now avidly exercise and eating more protein. My bone density improved 4.7% over 2 years!

And now with grandkids ages 17 to 3yo, I want to take them places but they are too busy with high school sports that train and compete during school breaks and even practice during the summer!

I enjoy going places but with the family/grandkids, otherwise I am good with just watching a National Geographic special.

Trips/activities to build memories with the family, the cousins-times are a priority. But should have timed it before high school sports!

Well, done getting your bone density up! How did you do it? Was it mostly protein and exercise? Did you measure it with a DEXA scan? I’m in a dad bod challenge and just got my scan this past weekend. I’m gonna write about it soon.

Grandkids have to be an amazing motivator! I hope to live long enough to have them myself. I love being a dad :)

Doing a dexa once every 6 months has been great – albeit don’t take too much from the scan in so far as accuracy. It’s best to just compare it to the ones before for improvement. Make sure u follow same timing and protocol and the numbers can be “gamed”

Maybe im nuts, but im 54 work out 5-6x a week, play baseball/softball 3-4 days a week during good weather, and do martial arts 2-4 times all while working F/T. Kids are out of HS and either in college or graduated and the amount of time that I have back to myself and my wife needs to be filled – and it won’t be watching TV or going to bars.

I don’t see myself ever slowing down but of course I will, but def dispute the slow-go age bracket – being an empty nest opens up a lot of possibilities.

Big time home upgrade with 10 years left until retirement. Figured it’s now or never. Breaking a couple of your 30/30/3-5 rules to do so, but like I said, it’s probably now or never after waiting to climb to the top of the property ladder for the past 20 years. Move also allows adult son to be with us for a few more years while he saves for his own place.

And you wish you had purchased the nicer home when your son was still living at home with you as a kid?

I’ve decided the best time to own the nicest house you can afford is when you have the most number of heartbeats at home.

aah Monopoly, the game that makes tempers rise and tantrums rife. Many a yougster has thrown a fit and stormed off in a rage in my family playing this ‘family game’. And as an adult I was shocked on another level when my sister in law teamed up with my brother during a game to thwart me. I only just managed to resist throwing a tantrum. That backhanded alliance still burns. 2 to 1 chess sounds great! What fun! My gran loved doing crosswords. Her sideboard was always strewn with The Oford Dictionary, other dictionaries, thesauruses and many other helpul aides. (no electronic devices used). She was very active and involved in life and lived to a spritely 97. She always compared the price of things to her War Ration book. That always made ne smile. My dad’s only birthday wishes every year was for ‘Peace and Quiet’. Now I find myself wishing for quiet and peacefulness quite a lot! He never retired, had his own consultancy business and worked into his 70s. But he played golf all the time, he loved it. So, follow your passion and do what you love is key. And be careful who you play Monopoly with.

Glad to know my six-year-old daughter is not the only one throwing monopoly pieces! Haha.

I have Long for peace and quiet since I was 40 years old. And that longing has noted. I will never live in a busy neighborhood full of restaurants and bars close by ever again.

For sure, not to wait until retirement to travel overseas while one is still active, quite fit and highly mobile. As long as one is not depleting money for basic retirement living daily expenses, travel during your middle career years onward. One thing I didn’t plan initially is also scheduling courses and paying for them plus travel dates around all this in retirement.

A good 87 yr. old friend and long divorced grandmother sold her condo 5 years ago and moved from another province to be closer here to son and adult grandchildren. Her previous 2-bedroom condo was snapped up for $900.000 by a … 90 yr. In metro Vancouver. Woman in her wheelchair since it was on ground floor. Unexpectedly fast sale.

Wasn’t it Sophocles that celebrated the loss of (physical) passion in old age? It brings clarity and diminishes the distraction of fleeting pleasures.

Growing up in the 80’s and early 90’s in the Midwest, all I really wanted was a Mustang GT. When choosing a major at university, I would compare the average starting wages to the cost of a new Mustang. For better or worse, I was very good at delayed gratification, and I always found a good reason not to get the Mustang — first graduate school, then saving for retirement, then building a non-retirement portfolio; getting married, getting a house, having children. At some point it dawned on me that I could easily buy a dozen new Mustang GTs, and while it might be fun for a few months, it most certainly would not move the needle on the happiness meter. So I threw away that old desire. The lesson I took away was that if you delay gratification long enough, for all but the most important things you will eventually realize you don’t really need (or even want) it anyway. Maybe this is where a lot of older folks end up.

My parents had no money, and so spent no money in retirement beyond the basics, and perhaps spoiling their pets. My in-laws lived it up through their mid-70’s in terms of seeing the world, and then became homebodies when their health started failing in untreatable ways. My wife and I traveled quite a bit before having children, and we’ll probably do so again after the kids are grown, but I already find travel less exciting than before, so I’m sure at some point I’ll just prefer staying home. Some people might look on that with pity, but if someone is happier at home reading the paper, walking the dog, tending their garden, and (fingers crossed) playing with their grandchildren, what’s the point of spending extra money if it brings no marginal increase in happiness?

The real concerns of not spending joyfully of their healthy assets even after setting aside money for nursing care, is only for a small portion of folks. Meaning folks who have more than ie. 2-3 million $$ (not including their home).

Probably those of us are trying to balance between some nice things annually or every 2-3 yrs. vs. Saving for nursing care.

That said, as someone who has been carfree for last 40 yrs., I still happily ride my geared 20 yr. old bike. Yes, I could buy a more expensive new bike but it will mean I change my bike components to deter bike thieves despite bike locks. I did stop 2 different thieves in last 8 yrs.

This yr. far more slacker on foreign travel with spending only 1/4 travel money spent by travelling only in Canada which is still big enough to explore and at times, more expensive because it is the 2nd biggest country in world.

Agree the go-go years can start after 40-45 if one has a portfolio chugging along upward slowly and already live/own a home. Yes, that can be when career accelerates also. But honest, if one has enough vacation piles up Annually: use it well with travel. Am so grateful I joined my late partner on our own multi-wk. bike trips with our panniers in my mid-30’s to early 60’s. He retired early 58 and did go solo cycling trips during the time I was still happily working in my career.

Not sure if this is partially affecting my meh attitude about foreign travel. Next yr. To check if I snap out of my complacency.

Agree, elderly care cost is HUGE. Folks need to budget accordingly:

The Shocking Cost Of Elderly Care Most People Underestimate

I agree elderly costs are potentially huge. But note the word “potentially”. You could also die suddenly at 80 of a heart attack as many do, or pass away rather quickly from aggressive cancers. I know folks are paralyzed to spend because are self-insuring possible long term care and think they will need millions set aside. That is like not spending because there may be another 1929 market crash. OK its possible but not a way to live life. Don’t waste your life living for the unlikely.

Lets say we do think about the very unlikely – that you and your spouse will need dementia related long term assistance for three years each. Good care is about 15k per month – with no insurance. 15k x72 = 1.080M. Again no insurance and 3 full years for both of you.

If you are planning to self-insure setting aside that much is reasonable (still very very safe), but more than that is not reasonable.

My mother has also lost interest in a lot of things. She’s also quite a disagreeable person which certainly doesn’t help. But when I went to visit her earlier this year after a long hiatus, she refused to leave the house. She didn’t want to go for a walk. Didn’t want to go out to a restaurant. Didn’t want to go out for any activity at all. Ten, twenty years earlier, it would be hard to keep her inside. She’s taken a complete shift to being sedentary and apathetic.

I think my hardest challenge as I age will be accepting inflation. I just can’t stand to pay for things that cost so much more than they used to. But I hope I will continue to pay for experiences. I won’t need much stuff down the road, but I really do want to maintain friendships and memorable experiences.

“I just can’t stand to pay for things that cost so much more than they used to.”

I call this the point when your economic clock breaks. After that, all prices become surreal to you. My grandfather’s clock broke around 1940, so if you told him in 1980 you made $30k/yr, he thought you were rich. The easiest way to assuage this is to play with an inflation calculator and run it 40 years into the future.

These friends who drive an 11 year old car while being worth 8 figures… you know that sounds just like an author I know of ;)

What a foolish guy! He’s gotta YOLO more!

I think this is not going to be a problem for almost anyone as end of life care will simply obliterate any assets people have left. The only exception to this will be the top five percent or so and given the continuing inflation in this sector, I’m not sure anyone outside the infamous 0.1% will have assets to pass down in the end.

I’m not sure things are that pessimistic.

About 65% of Americans own homes, and about 40% of those don’t have a mortgage. Real Estate has done quite well over the past 15 years.

Meanwhile, about 60% of Americans own stocks, which I’ve done even better.

Therefore, the majority of Americans have benefited from economic growth that they can pass on.

Have you not benefitted tremendously, especially since Covid?

“Have you not benefited tremendously…” Of course. However, I’m not yet at the age where people pay $250,000/yr for LTC. When I reach that point, it will likely be closer to $400k – $500k per year. For the at least 40% of Americans who will get LTC, I don’t see them dying with any assets to pass down.

Some die without ever needing any LTC, others die within the 100 days Medicare allows after a hospital stay, others die within one year of starting LTC. Maybe 20 percent will need more than one year of LTC.

Yeah, maybe 20-30% need up to 3 years. Not sure about 1 year, but 3 years is often the expected max based on the people I’ve spoken to in the industry. Better to be conservative for financial safety.

Sounds like your parents are entering their “Slow-Go” years after having a good run during their “Go-Go” years.

I’ve read that in retirement that there’s 3 phases:

Most folks talk about the retirement “smile” in terms of spending – spend most in the “Go-go” years doing everything you’ve always dreamed of doing; then spending drops in the “slow-go” years then rise again in the “no-go” years due to rising medical costs.

It’s great that you are constantly thinking of what you can do to spend time with your parents, even if they no longer have interest in activities they previously used to enjoy. However, another thing to consider is – are they actually content with their world & span of activities shrinking? Or are they falling into inertia, which could lead to greater risk of dementia / depression, etc?

I’ve seen that happen with my in-laws – where after a fall, my father in law refused to even leave the house for 7 months and just sat in his bedroom watching TV all day. He got very snarky and depressed and snapped at everyone so much that his friends eventually gave up coming to visit. He also lost his mobility (since he refused to walk more than a few steps from the bedroom to the bathroom and back). It was really tough for my mother-in-law as she was then stuck with him all day with no relief in sight.

It was only when we arrived to visit with the kids that we managed to get him motivated to even get out of the house. We spent a month with them and got him interested in activities again – and he started walking, going to the library, meeting friends, going to the seaside or the forest (which he used to love before his fall). Part of it was his motivation to see the grandkids, as we told him that our 6 and 3 year old had zero interest sitting indoors all day watching boring sports programs; and if he wanted to interact with them – he had to meet them at their level. Part of it was regaining his confidence in doing things even if it’s harder than it used to be. He’s since regained his mobility, interest in life as well as people around him.

My parents are the opposite, where they’re in their 70s and happily planning multiple trips both locally and overseas with their friends each year. This year alone, they’ve been to China (Silk Road), Tibet, Mongolia, Japan (twice), as well as numerous local trips just to check out a new train journey or new restaurant or new place. I’m sincerely impressed by their active lifestyle and hope that it continues long into their 80s. They’ve repeatedly told us that they know that their “Go-go” years are getting less, and they mean to make the most of it before they physically are no longer able. They also know that they’ve got more money than life/health span now; and are enjoying it while they can.

A great comment, and I’ve created a chart to help illustrate the point.

The exercise we do and the food we eat in our 40s 50s and 60s will help determine our health in our 70s.

Key is to make people realize this before it’s too late. Because as we all know, the path of least resistance is to do nothing.

#6. Personal Investments • Re: In retirement should the goal be just a Roth IRA?

If you are retiring before 65 and plan to use the ACA for health coverage, you need a minimum taxable income or you will get bounced to Medicaid. That happened to me the first year I applied, because I answered a question wrong, and I had to call the local Medicaid office to get disqualified again. There may be other situations where having some taxable income is desirable, and converting from pre-tax to Roth is an easy way to generate that.

#8. What Is the ‘Couch Economy’ Costing You?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Delivery, streaming and online shopping make it easy to live life from your living room. Keep costs in check with a solid strategy.

I get groceries delivered about three times a month. From my couch, I can also order dinner, buy a dress for an upcoming wedding and stream a movie. Many months, a solid chunk of my budget gets spent without me even leaving the house.

This is the new “couch economy,” according to a recent report from Visa.

In the couch economy era, more and more domestic spending is happening online — 58% in 2026 in the U.S., compared to 48% in 2019, based on Visa transactions. About a quarter of active U.S. Visa cards are used for 10 or more online or in-app transactions per month, a near-doubling since 2019.

“What we can see is a meaningful shift in how and where consumers transact,” said Mohamed Bardastani, principal CEMEA economist at Visa, in an email. “The strongest evidence is the rise in frequent online and in-app purchasing.”

Visa’s research doesn’t show whether people are spending more overall or whether these transactions are replacing other spending.

So is the couch economy good or bad for your wallet?

The couch economy shows us that hanging at home still offers plenty of ways to spend money, and people are jumping on board.

“We’re not just seeing consumers buy more goods online,” Bardastani said. “We’re seeing digital habits become embedded across shopping, entertainment, food delivery and other parts of everyday life.”

When digital spending is ingrained in your life, it’s easy to blow through your budget, since sites have made it possible to buy with one click.

“With online spending, there’s absolutely no friction and it’s really hard to keep track of,” says Corey Bates, an investment advisor representative at Solomon Financial in Carmel, Indiana. “If you’re not reviewing your budget and being intentional with your money, it’s really easy for it to slip away.”

At first glance, being able to shop, DoorDash dinner and stream at home seems like a great setup. (Jeeves, bring me my groceries.)

But it comes with a cost. When I use Instacart to buy groceries, I pay a service fee, a shopper tip and a markup on items at the store I usually order from. When I’m short on time, it may be worth it to me, but it’s not free.

“You’re saving some time, but you’re paying for it,” says Martin Lynch, president of the Financial Counseling Association of America.

Being a part of the couch economy doesn’t have to harpoon your budget. In fact, as long as you have a budget and your digital shopping life fits within it, you’re in good shape.

“I think you just need to have rules around it,” says Shampaigne Graves, a women’s consumer expert and founder of Women’s Research Solutions, a market research and sales strategy firm in Dallas.

For instance, she says, you might decide that a restaurant must be at least a few miles away before you order delivery from it. And you can audit your streaming subscriptions and keep no more than three per month, or whatever number works for you.

“These subscriptions are raising prices all the time,” Graves says. “But we aren’t necessarily checking our statement at the end of the month to see how that really impacts us.”

For Lynch, grocery delivery was worth the price when he broke his leg a couple of years ago. As the person in the family who bought groceries, he felt he could still contribute by doing the shopping online. “I could make my wife’s life easier,” he says.

Review a few months’ worth of transactions and add up fees and tips, plus check your subscriptions. If the number surprises you, make one change to bring it down, like shopping more in person or cooking more at home.

“Convenience has real value,” Bardastani said, “but consumers should still be thoughtful about which services are delivering value for them.”

#11. You’re Not Rich — And Neither Am I
