Warren Buffett has spent decades telling anyone who’ll listen that he lives simply. Same house in Omaha he bought in 1958 for $31,500. No mansion, no car collection, nothing flashy.

He eats at McDonald’s, drinks Coke by the case and has said more than once that a person could live like him on a fraction of his fortune and lose nothing that actually matters.

A physician two decades into a cardiology career already has a six-bedroom house on two acres with a three-car garage. Something that would put Buffett’s Omaha home to shame.

But Buffett flies private. On his personal jet. Which he owns. (He also owns the company that made his plane just FYI).

That cardiologist couldn’t touch a private jet with a ten-foot pole. Not on a $600,000 salary carrying a jumbo mortgage, two kids in private school and a home equity line he opened for the kitchen renovation.

Buffett could write a check for that physician’s entire house and still have money left for the furniture.

My point is, quantifying wealth is not a black and white endeavor. McMansions don’t lead to private jets. And “modest” lifestyles don’t rule them out.

It’s a strange world we live in. One where most people are blindly chasing perception rather than what actually matters.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Also read: Why Most Doctors Retire With Too Much Money (And What to Do About It)

The Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances states that the median American household net worth is $192,084. The average is more than 5x that at $1.06 million due to a relatively small number of extremely wealthy households that pull the average up.

Physicians, as a group, are ahead of that median and the gap keeps widening.

Medscape’s 2026 Physician Wealth & Debt Report found that 24% of physicians now report a family net worth of $5 million or more — largely thanks to stock market gains and rising home values.

However, the same report makes it clear this wealth isn’t evenly spread. The physicians in the $5 million group are mostly in procedure-based specialties which have the highest earning ceilings to begin with.

Plenty of physicians in lower-paying specialties spend most of a career well short of that mark despite carrying the same title, the same debt load at the start, and the same years of deferred income during training.

All physicians start with some sort of student debt — small or big — regardless of specialty. The median medical school debt for the class of 2025 is $215,000, not counting undergraduate loans.

Or any non-education debt, credit cards and car loans that tend to accumulate during residency for that matter.

A newly minted attending earning six figures can still have a negative net worth. It takes years to pay down debt and bring it up to zero.

Years more to enter the black. Those early years are the reason for the gap between a $5-million-net-worth radiologist and a physician twenty years into practice who still hasn’t crossed seven figures.

Let’s talk about two doctors who have the same degree and the same starting debt but two very different philosophies on spending money.

For this example we’ll play into the most common stereotypes doctors have faced — and fought hard to shed — for years.

Dr. Flashy “invests” in a new Range Rover every three years. He’s got a lake house two hours outside the city, a boat he uses maybe four weekends a summer — if the weather cooperates.

And surprisingly to some, he’s not broke. He makes real money and a part of his lifestyle is funded from that same income.

Almost every single one of these major purchases generates its own follow-on bill which continues to recur exponentially.

The Range Rover’s routine maintenance costs more than a lot of people’s monthly car payment. The lake house needs a new roof eventually, landscaping every season, comes with a property tax bill that rises every time the county reassesses and someone to physically check on it every time a storm rolls through three states away.

The boat comes with marina fees, winterizing and a marine mechanic who bills by the hour. Buying something nice is the equivalent of signing up for a subscription with an indefinite term and a rising rate.

This is called the hedonic treadmill. Once someone upgrades something in their life, the old version stops being satisfying, permanently. And the new version only delivers that same satisfaction for as long as the novelty lasts.

Eventually the purchase itself becomes pointless. It was the feeling of upgrading that felt good but that feeling fades fast enough that the next upgrade becomes necessary just to get back to the baseline.

Luxury goods are sneakily good at triggering this because so much of what they deliver is the status attached to the price tag. Any functional improvement or value they bring is usually beside the point.

Dr. Flashy’s income may be large. He might even be a neurosurgeon earning $829,161. But at some point his lifestyle needs additional funding to keep up. That’s when he turns to financing.

Eventually, the bank becomes something he is increasingly dependent on.

To be clear, I’m not speculating on his character. Forbes reports that the highest-income American households, those above the 90th percentile, carry the largest average credit card balances of any income group (over $11,000 on average) despite being the group least likely to carry a balance at all.

So data shows us that the people who look the most financially comfortable are disproportionately dependent on revolving debt to stay there. Not all high earners are predisposed to open lines of credit, but when they do, they tend to rack up more of it because the lifestyle they’re financing costs more to maintain than anyone else’s.

The thing is, money is finite even with a large income. Spending more of it means you need more just to sustain the spending at its current level. And that treadmill doesn’t slow down as the years go by.

Dr. Net-Worth has the same income as Dr. Flashy. Same specialty, even, same call schedule, same patient panel.

But Dr. Net-Worth drives a Honda he’s had since fellowship. It’s got a cracked bumper he keeps meaning to fix. He lives in a house that’s nice but completely unremarkable from the street — not something you’ll see featured in Architectural Digest.

Still, his investment accounts feature a sum that would make your eyes water. No one except him and his accountant know what it is.

We have come to perceive net worth as some concrete evaluation of a person’s wealth. But it really isn’t. In fact, the more zeroes it has, the less real it is.

I mean, this year we saw Elon Musk become (briefly) the first ever trillionaire. But does that mean he’s got a Scrooge McDuck vault full of gold coins stacked to the ceiling?  Well, he might — but he won’t have an actual trillion in there to dive into and swim around in.

That number is mostly the market’s opinion of his equity stakes on a given day. An opinion that can — and does — swing by tens of billions of dollars before lunch and back again by dinner. All without a single dollar changing hands or a single decision on his part.

Dr. Net-Worth’s number works the same way just on a smaller scale. Most of it lives in a house he’s still making payments on every month, a retirement account he can’t touch before a certain age lest he trigger a penalty, and an ever-growing brokerage account he could never imagine drawing from.

All of it is his. Yet, he doesn’t use a dollar of it beyond the mortgage payment and the grocery bill. He’s rich! Technically. Psychologically, it might as well be someone else’s money.

You can’t fault him for being this way. Sometimes it’s just temperament. Plenty of high earners are simply frugal by nature, genuinely uninterested in the lake house and actually happier to keep the Honda running for another hundred thousand miles. Nothing wrong with that. At least Dr. Net-Worth doesn’t need rescuing from the life he has chosen.

But sometimes the hesitation to spend stems from fear. Constant worry that the money could vanish overnight, that one bad market year or one malpractice suit could erase everything you’ve built.

That spending on anything beyond the bare essentials is an invitation for disaster to strike. Dr. Net-Worth worked his butt off to build a financial fortress that classifies him as financially free. Yet the day may never come when he actually gets to taste that freedom.

Dr. Flashy is one bad year/one slow season at the practice/one unexpected repair bill on the boat away from a very uncomfortable conversation with a lender.

Dr. Net-Worth has already won the game by any objective measure but refuses to enjoy it.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Financial planner Derek Hagen says that money that isn’t pointed at anything in particular just accumulates, and accumulation without a purpose behind it isn’t freedom. Dr. Net-Worth has plenty of money with no real purpose for it.

Dr.  Flashy has an answer: status and visible proof that he has “made it”. But his answer costs more to maintain with every passing year, never quite delivering the sense of arrival he’s chasing.

There’s no handbook that outlines exactly where the divide between enjoying the money and hoarding it is. And anyone who claims there is one wants to sell you something.

You, the physician reading this, are probably nothing like Dr. Flashy or Dr. Net-Worth. And asking which one is better or worse isn’t the point either.

Your money, no matter how it is accumulated or spent on, deserves to be used to fund a life you chose on purpose. Not one assembled by accident out of habit, fear or…what the neighbors might notice.

Buffett kept the house and bought the plane because both of those choices added up to a life he actually wanted. That is rich (of course being worth $144.6 billion doesn’t hurt).

Everything else is just perception in a strange world that will never stop raising the bar.

Of course, $5 million in a West or East Coast city means something entirely different than $5 million in a medium sized town in the Midwest or South. By way of information, if anyone is interested in how their assets compare relative to the U.S. net worth figures (by age, education or region), more information can be found here: https://dqydj.com/net-worth-percentile-calculator/

Also, in another 6-8 weeks, the Federal Reserve Bank will issue the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finance (SCF), which presents its own set of (updated) net worth and income figures.

The lingering question is – how do you determine the net present value of future social security payments or a pension, if eligible for one? Do you include that in a net worth statement or not?

The takeaway I have this article is to be neither a hoarder nor a ‘flashy’. Be comfortable in your spending style. And, in spite of the stress of the medical profession, it is good to practice gratitude for the opportunities to serve and have a roof over our heads.

Btw, I think the US government is going to face financial headwinds over the next 10 years. Social security and Medicare are going to run out of money (2032, 2033). In 2027, a large number of long-term bonds are going to mature and need re-financing. The real details can be found on the web, but you have to go digging for them. Carpe Diem.

#12. The Shockingly Simple Math Behind Social Security

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who currently draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

Those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

That little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:

If you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

In between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

First let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:

When you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:

At that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be big enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re new to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

What this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:

Whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result!  Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

To really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a big lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:

So the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

And of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

The net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:

Can we just put this in ONE SIMPLE TABLE based on some reasonable assumptions?

Yes, absolutely! Just to hit the most common situation, let’s assume a household that has

How much is this future benefit worth you you, based on your current age?

These aren’t enormous FAT Fire numbers, but every one of them is enough to feel like a meaningful contribution to your eventual early jump into freedom. For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a big boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

Sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all issues. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Log yourself into ssa.gov, and if it’s your first time doing that – congratulations! Note that new users will need to create an account, and they’ll guide you to login.gov for that purpose. Don’t fret, it’s very useful to have this account for multiple reasons.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions

If you log in to check on your Social Security account when you’re still young, you’ll see some confusing stuff – basically it tells you how much your payout will be if you continue working and contributing for a ridiculously long 35 year period!Your benefit is calculated by taking an average of your 35 highest years of earnings, which sounds bleak for people like me who only worked a ten-year career, because in theory that average might contain mostly zeroes. But never fear because:

To illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35.  Look at the difference in their benefits:

So the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the big earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI

Even though this has become a long article, it is still far from a complete analysis of the Social Security program. If you want to learn more, I’ve found the AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude, Google Gemini or OpenAI’s Chat GPT) to be shockingly useful at answering questions and running analyses. If you haven’t started using these in your financial research, I highly recommend them. Just search for any of those names (or install the phone app), start typing your questions, and you’ll be learning at a rapid pace within moments.

This Net Present Value framework completely changes the math for me. As an active investor, I’ve been weighing whether to claim early and invest the checks or wait.

I turn 64 this November, and by delaying just one year, I effectively ‘buy’ a guaranteed, inflation-indexed ~7% bump in my benefits for life. In today’s market, where valuations feel ‘rich’ and finding a low-risk 7% return is tough, I’ve decided to apply some ‘valuation discipline.’

I’m following Warren Buffett’s lead here—holding some cash and waiting for a ‘fat pitch’ or a market correction, all while letting my Social Security asset grow safely on the sidelines at a rate the market can’t currently guarantee. Thanks for providing the framework to look at it this way

How long have you been sitting in cash? Your post is dated April 16, 2026 meaning you could have bought the 10% dip in March 2026. Now the market is up 20% since then.

There are thousands of articles on how and why market doesn’t work, but some people still like to try.

Probably better to just pick a long term asset allocation you are comfortable with holding forever.

Any “gains” you are getting by delaying social security are now lost due to your failed market timing. Hoarding cash only works if you are willing to deploy it.

That said all the planning that we do with SS, age of retirement, investments etc. is still valid because one is minimizing the losses due to inflation. Something that really helped me with the mental math of Social Security is the concept of bend points.

Bend points are lifetime earnings milestones that govern how much Social Security pays out to you. For all income up to the first bend point, you get about 90 cents back from Social Security for every dollar you pay in. After that, it drops off steeply. For income between the first and second bend points, you get more like 32 cents on the dollar, and after the second bend point, you get about 15 cents.

Right now in 2026, you hit the first bend point at something like $540,000 of total lifetime earnings, and the second bend point is around $3.25 million.

The great news for early retirees is that, because Social Security’s payout formula tails off so quickly for higher earners (as you mentioned in the article), it really doesn’t matter very much that we won’t have 35 full years of contributions. Just by working a few years, we get most of the benefits. After that, it’s a game of diminishing returns where you have to work for years and years just to increase your benefit by a small amount. No thanks – I’d rather be retired!

Great question.. in the equations I showed in this article, they don’t show that more complex calculation: they are only showing how to calculate the present value of a stream of payments as it would apply *right now*.

To get the full value you need to calculate “the net present value of a 30 year stream of inflation-adjusted $5000 per month payments that starts 30 years from now”

So you’d solve the simpler equation first to get the NPV for that stream of payments on whatever day it starts, and then re-apply the NPV formula for a fixed chunk of future money, brought forward to today.

Social security Whoa Nellie! Yes, of course you can start taking SS at age 62. As mentioned above, if you have taxable income above about $22,000, then $1 of SS is withheld per $2 of earnings above the $22,000. Not to worry, when you reach your full retirement age, you get the withheld money back. But those withheld dollars can’t be invested from age 62-67. Next, you can’t just “toss your SS check into an index fund and make 6% after inflation.” First, those capital gains might be taxed at 0, 15, or even 20%. More importantly, those are not guaranteed. Social security goes up 8% per year of delayed filing, PLUS inflation. And those increases, unlike the aforementioned index funds, are not subject to taxation along the way. So filing early and index funding vs delayed filing is comparing a speculative taxable strategy with a guaranteed tax deferred strategy.

It’s not taxable income that counts towards the $22,000, it is earned income. The two can be quite different (think dividends, interest, capital gains vs. salary).

You can certainly include NPV of SS in your Net Worth Statement. It is an Asset (it has monetary value). An asset doesn’t need to be immediately convertible to cash in order to count as an asset – there are simple examples such as a house (that takes time and has costs associated in turning the asset into ‘money’) and more complicated ones like REITs and annuities. They are all Assets as they have monetary value.

What is probably more logical to do is including SS as a Retirement Asset – or those assets you plan to live off of in retirement. This is often a different list of assets than what is in your Net Worth Statement – and is used for a different purpose (creating a stream of cash to live off of in retirement).

I’ve always questioned the “better to wait to withdraw for maximum benefits” position. That may be true for non-mustachians who need every dollar of SS to live on and are willing to work longer to maximize their annual income. But SS’s early and delayed adjustments are actuarially derived to ensure the total cost to the system is the same. Theoretically, you would receive the same amount over your lifetime. Claiming earlier is a hedge against dying young. Unless you have a crystal ball and are assured of living longer than average, it’s better to claim early and invest. I looked into this a few years ago, and came across the paper: https://crr.bc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/IB_19-18.pdf

It’s a great summary of the history of delayed and early options (early claiming was originally designed to allow the younger spouse to not be penalized for retiring with the older spouse). It also analyzes whether the assumptions for the original actuarial adjustments apply today. Summary: adjustments for taking early (65) are probably right. It’s a wash to take anytime after 65. However, higher earners live longer and delay more. If delayed adjustments were based on those who actually use it, the increase should be less. Based on increased life expectancies, wealthier individuals should wait.

I want to call out a couple considerations around the longevity of Social Security and Medicare for those in the USA.

First, there is a provision within the Social Security legislation that stipulates should Social Security funding be deficient to pay out all intended benefits, it will still pay out based on its annual tax intake. While the Social Security funding is quickly dwindling, the expectation is that the annual tax intake will continue to represent ~80% of intended benefits. Thus, even if you don’t expect Congress to actively fix Social Security funding, unless you expect Congress to actively kill Social Security then you should expect some payout.

That said, it is important to note that Medicare has no such deficiency stipulation in its legislation, so if Medicare funding becomes deficient then without an active effort from Congress it will just be gone. I know that early retirees typically plan for medical coverage between retirement and becoming Medicare eligible, but I’ve seen many assume Medicare will be there, which it may not. On one hand, ACA coverage creates a cost-capped option at age 65+, but that assumes that ACA coverage is still around. I know MMM has also suggested options such as self-funding or community plans, but I’ll warn that those are generally more viable for those early retirement years and become generally less viable for many as you get into your golden years. This is where HSAs can be really helpful, and since they can double up as 401k-like funds for non-medical expenses after 65, I really do recommend taking advantage of them as best as you can. Everyone’s costs and longevity will vary, and potentially significantly so if you require long-term care, but there is a general rule of thumb of trying to have ~$200k/person at age 65 bucketed for retirement medical expenses (premiums and out-of-pocket costs), where the expectation is that bucket should continue to grow despite withdrawals in the early years and then transition to mostly drawing down as you get further up in the years.

Please consider using a discount rate that meets the criteria of the “next best option of similar risk.” That is standard practice for discount rates. In this case, TIPS would be a natural choice. Their inflation-adjusted discount rate would be ~2%.

Using the proper 2% instead of 6% would lead us to the opposite conclusion as this article. That is, claiming at 62 is the WORST choice if you’ll live until 90.

I realize this might torpedo the entire article. But it’ll also lead the audience to reach better retirement conclusions.

I’m excited to see this topic! Most people I ask (including financial advisors and moneywise folks) insist that it’s almost always better to defer drawing Social Security until normal retirement age (67) or even later (70). However, most people don’t understand the time value of money! I retired four years ago at age 57 and I’m very much looking forward to drawing Social Security next year at age 62. Why? Because it’s a much, much better deal. Here’ s how it works. Using the data provided to me by the Social Security Administration, my current estimated monthly benefit amounts will be $2,513 if starting at age 62, or $3,569 if starting at age 67, and $4,425 if starting at age 70. It appears obvious that it would be best to wait for the higher amount. But it is not. Here’s why. In a zero-interest rate world, I can run a simple break-even analysis and determine that it would take me until age 78½ to come out ahead by waiting until 67 to start. It would take me until age 80½ to break even if I waited until 70 to start. With a current life expectancy for me to live until age 76½, I’m still better off to start at age 62, but only slightly. But then again, we don’t live in a zero-interest rate world! In a 4% interest rate world, these figures change dramatically. It now takes me until age 85½ to break even when starting at age 67, and until age 87 when starting at age 70. In an 8% interest rate world (The S&P 500 has averaged 10.5% annually since 1957), my break-even points are both now out beyond 100 years old. It’s really a no-brainer!

Hey Pete, Regarding your comment on you won’t care about the taxes on your RMDs when you’re 75 because you’ll have plenty of income. I take issue with that as a 75 year old with a six figure retirement income living a comfy life in expensive Boulder County like you. I don’t want to pay taxes to a federal government that is spending in areas that are not my values. But that’s not my main point. Only a couple people have commented on SS taxability (e.g., Jiri, Dave) aside from taxes on RMDs. Not everyone realizes that up to 85% of your SS income is taxable depending on what other kinds of annual retirement income you have. The IRS uses a formula where tax-deferred pensions, royalties, 401K distributions, and any earned income can trigger the taxability of your SS payment. The way to potentially avoid this with the present laws is to pay taxes on any future funds when you’re working, i.e., Roth contributions, Roth conversions, and backdoor Roths if you’re over the Roth eligibility limits. This works best for 1099 people, but W-2 people also can benefit from it to a lesser extent. I’m a believer it’s not how much you make, but how much you keep from the government.

However, if you are a high earner in your working years, it makes sense to max the traditional retirements accounts to avoid a (currently) 24% or 32% tax rate (which was actually quite a bit higher in the past), not worry as much about Roth, and then pay the tax on Social Security. Odds are that the tax on your Social Security will fall in the 12% bracket, or maybe 22% if you are making particularly substantial withdrawals from traditional retirement accounts.

The 4% rule is shockingly simple math, Social Security is not. (as evidenced by the fact someone very good at math – yourself – made a couple mistakes here that you had to correct!).

One thing that I’m surprised this didn’t mention is the “bond effect” of the SS PV. After reading this article I did a search for “social security present value” and came across this article from Michael Kitces: https://www.kitces.com/blog/valuing-social-security-benefits-as-an-asset-on-the-household-balance-sheet/

He discusses treating the lump sum value of the SS benefit as a bond allocation in the portfolio. I get why people might say “I don’t want to think about/consider SS because I’m so young”, but I think considering it might help people make better asset allocation decisions.

Take the 30 y/o couple in your example. If the PV of their projected SS benefit is $98k and they also have $200k invested (in retirement accounts and brokerage) then their asset allocation is roughly 33% bonds and 67% everything else. If they decide to start putting part of that $200k into bonds, then they may very likely be substantially over-allocated with bonds.

I scrolled looking to see if anyone had mentioned Kitces! I found it interesting to compare MMM’s article to this Kitces article (the case for delaying) (https://www.kitces.com/blog/how-delaying-social-security-can-be-the-best-long-term-investment-or-annuity-money-can-buy/)

How does MMM have higher SS benefit than me when he worked ~10 years and I worked 13 years at near max SS tax? Oh, he’s earned SE income for 15 of 21 retirement years. Lol. I hear sirens… oh, it’s the Internet Retirement Police. ;)

Useful tip – the SSA website has a calculator (once you login) where you can set your future annual salary to 0, to forecast what your true SS amount will be if you’re an early retiree without 35 years in their record yet.

Also interesting – apparently the max benefit is about $4200 at 67 if you worked 35 years at max SS taxation. That’s quite the NPV. (But also 35 years of work, ugh!)

In the Facebook comments about this article, someone was complaining about the low return that SS gives to high earners. His numbers were way off, but even if you do them correctly they are interesting: If you invest your max SS contribution at historical stock returns of 7% after inflation, you end up with $3.5M at retirement, which is good for about $11,000 per month rather than the $4200 the system gives us. Which sounds bad, but guess what, you can do both!

Math PhD here. Have been following this for 20 years I think, big fan. Retired exactly 2 weeks ago, age 58.

#13. Buy The Finished Home, Skip The Remodeling Misery

At almost 50, I’m never doing a gut remodel again.

Everyone who has survived one has the same thousand-yard stare. It’s the look of someone who spent two years arguing about grout color and waiting on inspectors who never show up when they say they will.

Remodeling might be the most unpleasant thing you can voluntarily sign up for. Nobody makes you do it. Yet every year, homeowners line up to hand over hundreds of thousands of dollars for the privilege of being miserable.

Cost overruns are common. So are time overruns.

If you’re brave enough to build a house or do a gut remodel, budget for the project to cost at least 50% more and take 50% longer than expected. If you do, you might come out only slightly bloodied and bruised. If you don’t, and you trust your general contractor’s estimate, your silent stress will go through the roof and detonate every relationship around you.

Here’s a great chart compiled by ResiClub from a report by University of Chicago and Princeton professors titled “Where Is It Slow To Build, And Is It Getting Slower?”

I’m not shocked to see San Francisco at #1, averaging 1.1 years to get a permit and 3.8 years to build a single-family home. San Francisco, after all, is the most expensive city to raise a family.

Miami and Philadelphia are close behind at about 3.4 years, while Indianapolis, El Paso, and Colorado Springs get it done in roughly six months. The national average from permit application to completion is about 8.8 months.

So a San Franciscan could watch a family in Indianapolis build seven homes in the time it takes to finish one. And it’s getting worse. Nationally, single-family permitting time roughly tripled from 1.6 months in 2000 to 4.9 months in 2023.

I’ve gone through two gut remodels and a couple of bathroom remodels since first buying San Francisco property in 2003, and every one has been a hellish process.

My last gut remodel started in mid-2019 and wasn’t 100% done until the end of 2022. Granted, COVID delayed completion by about six months. But three years for a project I thought would take one year at most was brutal.

At least I was able to run out the upstairs portion of the house while the ground floor gut remodel languished.

Here’s what most buyers miss. The construction bill is only the visible part of the iceberg.

Let’s say you buy a $1.6 million fixer and budget $400,000 for a gut remodel over 18 months. Reasonable, right?

Now apply reality. The budget runs 50% over, so it’s $600,000. The timeline stretches to 2.5 years. Meanwhile, you need somewhere to live. At $6,500 a month in rent, that’s $195,000. You’re also paying roughly 1.2% in property tax on a house you can’t live in, about $48,000 over 2.5 years.

Add it up and your $1.6 million fixer actually cost you about $2.44 million. And I haven’t even counted the opportunity cost of tying up roughly $850,000 in cash that could have been compounding in stocks or private investments.

Then there’s the cost you can’t put on a spreadsheet. If your kids are five and seven when you start, they’re eight and ten by the time you move in. You don’t get those years back living out of boxes in a rental while texting your GC at 10 pm.

If you’re over 40 and plan to buy in a city where building takes longer than 1-1.5 years, I highly encourage you to buy a fully remodeled home. You’ll save so much time, money, and headache.

At least in San Francisco, the market undervalues fully remodeled homes. Given how painful remodeling is, they should trade at much bigger premiums than they do. I suspect the same is true in most slow-to-build cities. Take a look at this illustrative chart.

In this hypothetical example, ten years ago, buying a fixer and remodeling it yourself may have saved you roughly $250,000 compared to buying a finished home. That was real money for the pain.

Today, the savings have shrunk to about $60,000. Labor costs, material costs, and permitting delays keep eating away at the discount, while finished homes haven’t gotten much pricier relative to fixers.

Spread $60,000 over 2.5 years of construction and you’re earning about $2,000 a month to manage contractors, chase inspectors, and live in a rental. And that assumes nothing else goes wrong. One bad subcontractor or a three-month permit delay and the savings disappear entirely.

How hard could it be, they ask themselves? Get an architect, hire a reputable GC, pay them to pull permits, pick out the fixtures, and you’re good to go.

But unless you’ve gone through a full remodel or ground-up build, you have no idea how hard things are and how long they take.

Here are some examples of the frustration:

The list goes on. What can go wrong will go wrong, and all you can do is react.

The people working on your house will not operate under the same rules that you do. All it takes is one person or one part to mess the entire remodeling process up.

Do not underestimate how painful remodeling or building is. Your college degree or fancy job title means nothing.

The second reason is more understandable, especially for quirky rich people. Most fully remodeled homes are designed to appeal to the most buyers possible. White oak floors. White quartz countertops. Gray accent walls. Matte black fixtures. Tasteful, safe, and about as exciting as plain oatmeal.

If you want a jade green kitchen, a speakeasy behind a bookshelf, or a Japanese soaking tub with a view of the fog rolling in, no developer is building that for you. You’ll have to do it yourself.

I get it. Your home should reflect who you are. But ask yourself how much you’re willing to pay to express yourself. Paint, lighting, furniture, art, and landscaping can get you 80% of the way to a unique home for a fraction of the cost and time. And the more personalized your remodel, the fewer buyers will want it when it’s time to sell.

Your dream home might be someone else’s gut job.

After all my remodeling experience, I’ll gladly pay a hefty premium for a fully remodeled home and live with someone else’s beige taste. Thankfully, the market hasn’t priced these homes at ridiculous premiums… yet.

Stop being so eclectic and picky. Buy the finished home and then make cosmetic changes if you want.

The noise bullet point is worth a closer look, because it goes both ways.

When you remodel, you’re the villain. Your crew shows up at 8 am with saws and jackhammers, and the retiree next door who just wants a quiet afternoon nap starts plotting against you.

I know because I’m that retiree now. As I wrote in the one negative of living in a nicer neighborhood nobody talks about, five neighbors around me have been doing major remodels in less than a year.

Nicer neighborhoods attract buyers with the money and ambition to rip everything out. So even if you buy a remodeled home, you’re not fully escaping construction. You’re just escaping the bill.

I’ll take that trade any day. Here's a podcast episode I did (Apple, Spotify) talking to my friend Harry on his new home building process.

Some of you will ignore me. That’s fine. It took me two gut remodels to learn this lesson myself. If you’re going to do it, at least do it smart:

The silver lining of any remodel is that when it’s finally done, you’ll feel relieved and maybe even thrilled to have survived the gauntlet.

It’s like hitting yourself in the head with a hammer. It feels amazing when you stop.

Even if your GC and subcontractors do everything right, they still have to get through the plumbing, electrical, and building inspectors, each of whom may inspect twice before the work can be covered up. Once you’re through it, you’ll marvel at all the hard work that went into making your home beautiful. Few things are more satisfying after a long journey.

And if you remodeled thoughtfully, by adding livable square footage or staying within a reasonable budget, you’ll likely get back at least 80% of your money. In cities with wealthier buyers or a booming economy, you may get back over 100% of the cost while enjoying the home in the process.

Just don’t forget to count the years it takes off your life.

Readers, where do you live, and what’s it like remodeling in your city? Have remodeling timelines gotten longer or shorter? How has the cost of remodeling changed? And would you pay a premium for a fully remodeled home to skip the process altogether?

If you still want real estate exposure but never want to deal with permits, inspectors, or a GC who ghosts you, consider investing passively. One area I’m watching closely is the real estate behind AI. Every AI model needs physical data centers, and the biggest tech companies are spending hundreds of billions a year to build them.

Take a look at Fundrise, which manages over $3 billion for more than 350,000 investors and primarily invests in residential and industrial real estate in the Sunbelt, where valuations are lower and yields are higher. You can start with as little as $10, and the platform does all the work while you nap in peace. Fundrise is a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai.

Wow. That chart is mind boggling. Government red tape is sickening. I cannot imagine spending a year just on permits in SF.

I’m in the mountains of Colorado. We broke ground on our home in May, and we’re 3 days away from getting our certificate of occupancy. We’re 2 months ahead of schedule and we came in slightly under budget. We heard all the horror stories, how my wife and I would end up broke and divorced in the process, how it would take longer than planned, run over budget, etc.

My biggest advice is to vet and find great subs (not an easy task), and then treat them ridiculously well. We brought a grill to the build site and cooked out burgers, brats, steaks 3-4 days a week. We had coolers filled with ice and their favorite drinks daily. I ate lunch with them a few days a week to bullshit with them, learn about them, their families, etc. Multiple subs on multiple occasions told me they never get treated like this. We also set aside a budget specifically for cash tips to our subs.

Ultimately, though, we had a lot of luck on our side. Every sub is a gamble and we were fortunate that we loved every single one of them.

Simultaneously, we have friends building and they simply hired a GC and never even met their subs, even during the build. They’re over a year behind schedule and are now in a lawsuit against the GC for shoddy work from his subs.

The upside is lower supply and higher prices for existing, owners. So if you never have to, Remodel, you are good to go.

Absolutely spoil the subs. I too have cases of gatorade, beers iced down for the guys. I’ll go to them about 10 am and ask if they want pizza or sandwiches for lunch and deliver on site. Cash tips are very effective, i like to give them early in the project and several times throughout the project. And know when to give them their space. I mean think about it, food, beer, respect, and cash, does it get any more simple than that?

Giving out beer opens you to huge liability issues if someone gets hurt. Don’t spoil the subs and open yourself to losing everything when insurance doesn’t cover a catastrophic injury and they come after your assets.

Perhaps after 5 or 6pm, after the day is done? Beers are a nice gesture, and hopefully they’ll come back better the next day.

You do it your way, i’ll do it mine. Plenty to worry about in this world, giving beer to guys who work their butts off for me isn’t one of them.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

The program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive plan for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

While Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

MoneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

The “Never 100” rule and “Straight A” strategy have become cornerstones of my financial habits, helping me live below my means and automate my savings and giving. It was perfect for someone like myself who didn’t want a complicated, jargon-filled financial class – and wasn’t going to sign up for an intense ‘shame & blame’ session either.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

For those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most important thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

Dylan is a devoted husband, father, and Christian leader who serves in lay-ministry at Calvary Chapel of Westmoreland County. With a background in marketing for influential organizations such as The Navigators ministry and Highmark Health, he brings a unique perspective to his passion for developing practical discipleship tools. He lives in Greensburg, PA with his wife and two children.

#17. Personal Investments • Re: What basic questions to ask to TIAA advisor?

... I would ask about TIAA Traditional (liquid and illiquid); what passive (not actively managed) index funds (or equivalents) they have for the total US stock market, the S&P 500, and a broad international fund they offer; and what the expense ratios are. To quote Rick Ferri, I would strive for simplicity to the extent that is available.
As mentioned in the original question, the various flavors of TIAA Traditional Annuity in the various accounts may have different terms. The illiquid Trad Ann will have strict limitations on withdrawals, and these may differ among the different accounts.
The liquid Trad Ann should be very flexible, but do double check whether these might be good as money market equivalents.

IF there are other holdings, such as TIAA or other "brand" equity or bond funds, the offerings may vary a lot among the different accounts.
So it might be advisable to select the "best", even if it means having "stocks" in one account and "bonds" in another. Even if the holdings can't be 'moved' between accounts, it should be possible to arrange (selling and buying) to maximize the choices among the accounts.

Also: Make note if one or more of the accounts includes a "brokerage option'", meaning a possibly huge collection of mutual funds from many other fund families.
They may (or not) be "better" than TIAA's own offerings.

#18. A Cancun All-Inclusive Where Adults Get Their Own Resort

The adults-only Secrets was recently renovated, and Dreams next door is family-friendly.

Until I set foot in Secrets and Dreams Playa Mujeres Golf & Spa Resorts in Cancun, Mexico, the only all-inclusive I had ever been on was a cruise. I didn’t know what to expect — and honestly, as someone who loves an action-packed itinerary, I thought I might feel a bit bored from staying put. But I couldn’t have been more wrong.

Secrets is the adults-only resort, while Dreams is the family-friendly one, and they’re located side by side. Room rates at both resorts start at about $500 or 25,000 World of Hyatt points for off-season nights. That includes your meals, drinks and activities. Hyatt covered the cost of my stay, but the views here are my own.

During my stay, the properties’ activities — which come included in the room rates — gave me a packed itinerary. I saw sea turtles on a group kayaking excursion. I took a sunrise yoga class on the beach. I played tennis, pickleball and basketball on different courts. I walked out on the beach for sunrise and sunset. I basked in a hot tub. Because I visited in September, which is the off-season in Cancun, the properties were incredibly quiet and peaceful.

If you want a high-end escape — and a break from worrying about dining bills and other logistics — staying at one of these properties could be a splurge that makes sense.

Secrets Playa Mujeres Golf & Spa Resort, the adults-only resort, was recently renovated, reopening in early 2026. Dreams Playa Mujeres Golf & Spa Resort opened about a decade ago.Both sit within the private, gated community of Playa Mujeres, about 40 minutes from Cancun International Airport. Adults have access to both Secrets and Dreams properties, meaning more pools, restaurants, shows, gyms and other places to stretch your legs.

Dreams is the family-friendly hotel of the two. It has two major water slides, plus two separate splash pads that have a handful of smaller slides and water play features. I'm 34 years old with no kids, and I still rode the water slides.

Kids club activities were running constantly throughout the day, including supervised outdoor movie nights and MasterChef Junior-branded activities based on the TV competition series, including a Mystery Box Challenge and family cooking classes where parents and kids cook together.

Secrets, next door, is the opposite. No kids are allowed, making for a noticeably calmer atmosphere.

Secrets' rooms, fresh off that 2026 renovation, felt noticeably more current with a brighter color palette and a lot more natural light. Dreams' rooms were still lovely, but you can tell by the aesthetic that the resort is roughly a decade old. It had darker color schemes, plus some older fixtures.

If you're traveling sans kids, the rooms alone are reason to book Secrets.

One detail both resorts share, and one of my favorite small design touches of the whole trip: Each room has a little cubby built into the door for room service drop-offs. Instead of a staff member knocking and waiting for you to answer, they can just leave your order in the cubby and go. It’s a nice way to ensure you have fresh coffee waiting in the morning without anyone needing to disturb you if you decide to sleep in.

Secrets is generally the quieter resort, but both properties had plenty going on at the pool. The main pools on each side were consistently lively, with assorted games and activities running throughout the day like a guess-the-song contest hosted by a very amped-up DJ. And on the Dreams side, I spotted what looked like an in-pool version of a Zumba class.

Both sides have multiple hot tubs and pools, so if one is busy, you can easily move to another.

Again, I was visiting during low season, so it was quiet. On the Dreams side, which has the water park, the two popular big water slides never had more than a one- or two-person wait.

Beyond the pool, both resorts offer a handful of activities for no extra charge, such as a group bike ride and nature walks. I went on a kayaking excursion, which was about 30 minutes of paddling out and 30 minutes back, and got to see some sea turtles along the way. It was one of the best activities available, in my book.

I also went to the gym every day. The one on the Secrets side had a better variety beyond the usual cardio machines and dumbbells, including medicine balls and plyo boxes.

Both resorts put on a show most nights, similar to cruise ships. But the quality here was variable.

The acrobatic show felt like an awkward high school production of Cirque du Soleil, with performers struggling to do handstands at times.

On the other end of the spectrum, a mentalist-style magic show was one of the most impressive performances of that kind I've seen. The performer created illusions of guests being tapped on the shoulder without actually touching them and correctly guessed the numbers that audience members were thinking.

The nearly two dozen restaurants across both resorts span a range of cuisines, including Italian, Mediterranean and French.

Most of the waiter-service restaurants are only open for dinner. Meanwhile, a handful of pool bars and quick-service locations serve classic pool fare like burgers and nachos, or custom salads and sandwiches.

Each side also has its own small cafe for sandwiches, coffee, ice cream and pastries. Plus, waiters will bring food directly to your lounge chair. Nearly all of it is included in your room rate, aside from Ki' Ki' Che (more on that later).

The best dinner I had during my stay was at the Latin American restaurant Ayara on the adults-only side. Its menu is organized by region, pairing bright, raw fish dishes with Amazonian-inspired small plates and a section of dry-aged, charcoal-grilled cuts. I especially loved the Amazonian Bitter Cassava (crispy fried yuca, similar to fancy French fries). Ayara's aesthetic also complemented the food; the maximalist restaurant was filled with plants and bold, over-the-top wallpaper.

Ki' Ki' Che, a seven-course tasting experience, was more hit and miss. My expectations were high, since it’s the only restaurant on-site that costs more to access. You can get in by booking a minimum three-night Preferred Club stay at Secrets, or you can pay $150 extra per person.

The best course by far was the blue corn tetela (a triangular pocket made of corn from Oaxaca) filled with epazote butter, greens and smoked sausage from Yucatán. The sixth course was protein-heavy, consisting of beef tenderloin and short rib. Dessert was a carrot-based dish served with mascarpone, cinnamon and ginger, which made for a compelling surprise without being overly sweet.

The food quality and creativity were excellent, but the space wasn’t. Meals were served on a patio that could have been romantic, but the fans weren't strong enough to keep up with the heat, and multiple guests were visibly sweating through the roughly hour-long meal.

I’d still absolutely recommend you go if you have complimentary access (especially if the weather is pleasant). But don’t feel bad if you don’t. Stick to Ayara, and save your $150 for the steam room in the spa, where you actually want to get sweaty.

The two resorts also offer buffets, which reflect their different audiences. Dreams' buffet skews toward more French fries and other kid-friendly options with less sushi, while Secrets does the opposite.

Alcohol is also included with your stay, and there’s no shortage of bars. My favorite spot was Desires Lounge. When there’s a big game on, it can double as a sports bar.

Standard room rates at either resort run from about $500 to $1,000 per night after taxes and fees, depending on when you go. That price includes all your meals, drinks and entertainment.

Room rates at Secrets are often the same or lower than comparable rooms at Dreams. That's a little counterintuitive, since Secrets is the more recently renovated property of the two. Take the win, adults without kids.

Both resorts sell standard rooms as well as Preferred Club rooms, a more expensive option available across the Hyatt Inclusive Collection that gets you more amenities and high-end dining options. More on that in a bit.

Both resorts are bookable with World of Hyatt points. NerdWallet values Hyatt points at 1.8 cents each, making them the most valuable of any major hotel loyalty currency.

Both resorts are Category D properties, meaning that stays here run between 25,000 and 55,000 points per night for a standard room accommodating up to two people. There’s an additional charge for more guests in the room. But based on the rates I looked at, you could get about 2 cents per point from booking with rewards here, a solid value.

Preferred Club is an add-on that gets you more access to upscale amenities. It might be worth splurging on if you’d otherwise pay to rent a Bali bed (those cool, shaded day beds) at the pool, or dine at the properties' high-end restaurant Ki' Ki' Che.

The price of Preferred Club varies widely, though. We found that the cost to upgrade ranged from less than $100 per night (in which case, go for it!) to about $500 per night (I’d skip), in our October 2026 analysis of 148 room rates from the resorts with check-ins between October 2026 and March 2027. Regular rooms in Preferred Club average 25% more expensive (or $212 per night) than the equivalent room but without Preferred Club benefits.

Preferred Club also can get you rooms with cool features you won’t find in regular rooms, but these reservations get far more expensive. A room with a swim-out shared pool (yes, one conveniently attached right to your patio) averages 43% more, or roughly $400 more per night, than one without. A room with its own private pool averages 77% more expensive, or about $700 more per night.

When you pay the upcharge for Preferred Club, you gain access to the Preferred Club lounge, where they have food throughout the day, as well as premium liquors. I don’t see the real benefit since there’s food pretty much everywhere, and I’m not much of a drinker. But if you enjoy cocktails on vacation, it might be a good deal.

Other benefits include a premium check-in experience at that very lounge, which pretty much means you’re seated during the check-in process with a drink in hand. You also have access to exclusive areas on property, including a dedicated beach area and use of the Bali beds at the pool and beach. If you don’t spring for Preferred Club, you can rent one starting at $200.

Preferred Club guests also get exclusive access to the lazy river.

Preferred Club can also pay off if you jump on special offers, which vary. I’ve seen limited-time offers for a complimentary round of golf for Preferred Club stays on certain dates, for example.You also get access to restaurants at exclusive times, such as breakfast at Maris, the seafood restaurant, which then opens to all guests during lunch and dinner. That can be helpful, since the wait at the main buffet at breakfast can be surprisingly long sometimes; one time it took me about 20 minutes to get a table.

Preferred Club with Secrets lets you dine at Ki' Ki' Che during breakfast, which was one of my favorite meals of the whole trip. Both the huevos rancheros with steak (pictured above) and the Oaxacan omelette used top-tier ingredients and were so flavorful.

If you really don’t want to pay more for Preferred Club, book early. I noticed that Preferred Club rates were often the last to sell out. In many cases, there was no availability for regular rooms, but many Preferred Club options.

Secrets would be exceptional for a romantic getaway. (I saw two weddings on a single night!) Besides the serene setting, much of the planning and logistics come built in.

Dreams, on the other hand, felt tailor-made for multigenerational trips. An all-inclusive setup makes it easy to plan and coordinate a big group, where everyone can run on their own schedule and eat whenever they want without anyone having to coordinate meals or sort out who's paying for what.

What I especially liked: For something like a big family reunion, families with kids can book the Dreams side, couples without kids can book the Secrets side, and everyone can still meet up at Dreams whenever they want.

Secrets and Dreams Playa Mujeres are a splurge, but when you consider that the price includes food, drinks and activities, I'd say it offers great value — especially if you can book with Hyatt points.

If you're traveling with kids, Dreams Playa Mujeres earns its family-friendly reputation with its slides, splash pads and creative programming. If you're traveling without them, Secrets' recent renovation and adults-only calm make it the better pick.

Either way, you'll have plenty of activities and dining options, and you won't feel bored.
