#35. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:

Every time you log into the exclusive “reviewers only” Vine website, you’ll see different stuff available for the taking. Sometimes there is almost nothing worthwhile – you’ll search for “porcelain plates” and get endless pages of pink plastic disposable party plates instead. You look for a toaster for your kitchen but instead there will be just a toaster cover with a cat wearing a witch hat. WTF!?

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well)

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

Reduce your tax liability with the 50-20-0% rule for FMV

Mr. Money Mustache October 9, 2025, 1:55 pm

Excellent! Thanks JB – this is so useful that I will have to edit the article to include a link to that discussion on Reddit. For anyone reading it here: https://www.reddit.com/r/AmazonVine/comments/1iq0gze/reduce_your_tax_liability_with_the_50200_rule_for/

After you review every product, it’s is now a USED product and the FMV is greatly reduced. Remember we are all opening and using the products to review them

The 50-20-0% rule for used products is something on the lines of:

50% FMV for name brand products 20% FMV for off brand/non branded name products 0% FMW for things you use for “business purposes for review, are broken or damaged, and are consumables that can’t be resold after opening

Using this rule, let’s say you bought $1000 worth of non branded stuff, you’d reduce FMV by $800. As the remaining resale value of the used products is now $200 using the 20% rule. You’d patties on $200, not $1000.

Edit: You are welcome to claim Amazon’s reported ETV as hobby income. Just remember:

To maintain access to vine, we are required to “do work” (aka review 60%+ of products) to get access to the products. The process of reviewing an item, results in an adjustment to the fair market value after doing so. After you review the item, the “remaining” value is not the inflated ETV.

If you don’t understand accounting, you need to be very detailed with your CPA. If you can’t be bothered with some simple accounting, you are welcome to pay your marginal tax rate for your ETV as hobby income.

From all my research and extreme warnings from my CPA, this “50-20-0%” method is not a legally recognized tax strategy and carries massive audit risk.

The products we receive are legally considered non-employee compensation given to us in exchange for the service of writing reviews.

The IRS strictly requires taxpayers to report the Fair Market Value (FMV) of this compensation at the exact moment of receipt (though in practice, Amazon’s FMV is set at tine of ordering, not receipt).

Because you take immediate ownership of the item at its full value, opening and using it to write the review is legally considered personal use. Therefore, you cannot claim business depreciation or arbitrarily lower your 1099-NEC gross income for the “wear and tear” of opening your own compensation.

My CPA explicitly stated he will not file our taxes using fabricated internet depreciation formulas to arbitrarily lower a 1099-NEC.

Here is another discussion on the TurboTax forums where someone explains exactly why you cannot use this 50-20-0 rule and that there is no accepted way to manipulate the FMV of what you receive: https://ttlc.intuit.com/community/business-taxes/discussion/amazon-vine-1099-nec-schedule-c-deductions/00/3715093

The Vine program can easily cause a significant financial impact come tax season. Because Amazon issues a 1099-NEC, the IRS system automatically assumes this is business income subject to an additional 15.3% self-employment tax. When added to a normal ~25% income tax bracket, that creates a massive tax burden. For me, even living in Texas with no state income tax, I am still looking at roughly a 40% tax burden by default, which is brutal.

You can try to claim it as a hobby to avoid that 15.3% FICA tax, but overriding a 1099-NEC, moving it from schedule C to schedule 1, requires preparation to defend since the discrepancy because it can trigger an automated CP2000 notice.

For context, last year Amazon sent me a 1099-NEC with a massive $38,000 FMV for all my 2025 Vine items. (yes, the curse of making gold which means much more allowance and expensive >$100 items, such as a $1500 Gigabyte laptop amd $1k mini split AC, and a lot of other expensive gold exclusive items)

My CPA does not want to use the hobby declaration for that $38k because the sheer volume and daily review time makes it very hard to defend, even though I have not sold anything.

Beyond the tax classification, you must be extremely careful about Amazon’s published FMVs because they are often wildly inflated. Sometimes if you wait a few months, you will find that you could have purchased the exact same product outright for less cash than you are paying in tax liability through Vine.

This is why I am giving the warning that you have to do your homework before choosing things, sivh as checking price history and comparing to similar products. Buying outright means you only buy what you actually need, the item can be returned if you don’t like it, has a real warranty when it breaks, and you do not have to waste 30-60 mins writing a detailed review.

For example, I ordered a cold press juicer, even though I already own about nine other juicers, assuming the FMV was fair. I figured getting it for 40 cents on the dollar was a good enough deal. A few months later, the retail price dropped by about 75%. I ended up paying more in taxes for an un-warrantied, non-returnable item that I wasted an hour reviewing than if I had just bought it outright down the road.

In another instance, I selected a frozen drink slushie machine with an almost $300 FMV, meaning $120 in taxes for me. I spent a lot of time reviewing it, put it away, and then pulled it out months later to actually use it and found it was not freezing properly. I attempted to contact the seller but Amazon simply stated there is no warranty on a “free” product, making my $120 tax cost completely irrelevant. I also found that they replaced that product with a near identical model at a much lower, more competitive price.

I do not believe you can safely claim depreciation the way others have said, and even claiming hobby status to avoid the extra 15.3% FICA means going directly against Amazon’s 1099-NEC filing, requiring you to be ready to defend it. That said, I am now a much wiser Vine participant. I only select items that either have a $0 FMV or a very good one that is actually at or below actual value, and only if they are items that I actually need.

Actually, you don’t take “ownership” of the item until the 6-month mark, when you get the right of disposition, (if you cannot sell it nor give it away, you don’t own it). Before that the non-consumable item is the property of Amazon that you have been contracted to use & review in return for the compensation of the item in question at that 6-month mark. The item carries no value to you until then and when it does become yours, it’s value is depreciated from whatever FMV Amazon may set for a “new” item by virtue of its being used.

#36. The Silent Stress Of Taking A Family Vacation On A Razor’s Edge

A couple days before I published Broke Again At 49, my wife said going to Las Vegas over the long weekend would be a lot of fun.

I had floated the idea a couple weeks earlier. Unbeknownst to me, she then spent several hours over several days researching hotels, flights, shows, and costs to make it happen. The holiday was only nine days away, and she wanted to lock in good seats and better rates before they disappeared.

Normally, I’d be thrilled by this level of initiative. Vacation planning for four is not easy. The logistics alone are complicated, especially with food allergies and disruptive sleep patterns.

But I wasn’t thrilled. Between the time I brought up Vegas and the night she did all the planning, I got hit with another $25,000 capital call from a different venture fund.

So after she walked me through everything, at a total cost of between $6,000 – $7,000 I told her I needed to think about it. Understandably, she wasn’t pleased. I was the one who suggested the trip in the first place. She did the work. And instead of an enthusiastic thank you, she got a “let me get back to you.”

She also didn’t know I was about to publish a post announcing I was strapped for cash again. Ever since the advent of AI, she no longer edits my posts.

Every father wants to give his family the best life possible. I’m no different. It stings when I can’t deliver.

To her credit, my wife said she’d be fine with a staycation. That mattered a lot. It showed she understood our situation even though I hadn’t fully explained it. She also was aware that I've been longing to do something different for quite some time, and the long weekend gave us that chance.

A week went by, and I had gone through a money manifesting exercise and raised enough liquidity to meet future capital calls. I didn’t raise the money to spend it. But at least I knew my investment obligations for the next three-to-six months were covered, and that took a huge weight off.

Further, we compromised on three nights instead of four, saving about $1,000 – $1,500.

Ultimately, I said yes for one simple reason. I was the one who estimated a 30% capital call within 12 months. Instead, 46% got called in just six. That was my mistake, not theirs. I wasn’t going to make my family pay for my bad forecasting. Let’s go on a memorable adventure.

When you’re the provider and you mess up, you own it. Even if your intention was to invest for your children’s future, the people who had nothing to do with your decision shouldn’t be the ones absorbing the cost.

Before agreeing to the trip, I made myself a promise: no grief about the hotel, the shows, or anything else she picked due to money. Going on vacation and stressing about money every day is the worst of both worlds. You spend the money and still don’t get the joy.

We booked two adjoining rooms at the Palazzo so we could spread out instead of cramming four people into one room. Thanks to my wife, we got great seats to Blue Man Group, Cirque du Soleil, and Popovich Comedy Pet Theater, the show starring rescue animals. Closer seats were important to help our son see more clearly.

Tickets averaged between $450 – $500 per show for the four of us.

We also went to the Illusions Museum, the Flyover, and took a tour out to Red Rocks, which was spectacular.

For dinner, we went to Smith & Wollensky, a nostalgic spot where I used to dine in New York City while going through seven rounds of interviews at GS. The firm gave me a $100 daily meal budget during that time. We also went to Lavo for Italian.

The kids had a blast. Mission accomplished.

The night before Red Rocks, I played poker from about 9:40pm until 1:30am. I was doing fine until I lost $350 in a bomb pot. My full house got beat by a bigger full house after my opponent flopped top set. That’s poker. No crying at the casino.

I went to bed at 2am and promised my wife I’d be up by 6am to bring back breakfast before our 7:30am departure. My wife and daughter aren’t morning people. I am. I spent 13 years waking up before 5am in finance, so four hours of sleep felt manageable.

At one of the Red Rocks vista points, I asked my wife if she could take a few portrait shots of me for my newsletter or future media requests. I didn't have an updated profile picture since 2025. She said sure.

After snapping some shots, then I asked if she could raise the camera to my eye level, since she’s nine inches shorter, and switch to vertical. That’s when I noticed she was getting irritated. When she finished, she handed back the phone without looking at me.

I felt hurt. I thought it was a simple request.

It also stirred up an old feeling of being a burden. I almost never post pictures of myself because it feels superfluous and awkward. I don’t celebrate my birthday either, since it falls in June when school is out and everyone’s busy.

I’m the one who takes the pictures, which I enjoy. The footage is often a surprise when you look back, and it captures moments that disappear too fast.

So asking someone to take photos of me already felt uncomfortable, even if that person is my wife. Asking for retakes with directions felt worse.

With some distance, I've come to realize I'm the problem.

She had already taken a bunch of shots. Then I started giving camera direction like a fussy fashion photographer. Raise it. Turn it. Eye level. Vertical. On four hours of sleep and $350 lighter, my tone was probably more critical than I realized.

I should have just trusted her. She’s taken thousands of great photos of our kids. She didn’t need coaching.

And I bet she had her own stress. She planned the entire trip, got up early, wrangled two kids through a casino city, and was dealing with a husband who’d been quietly anxious about money for weeks. Being on the receiving end of that energy isn’t fun.

When you feel money stress, small interactions get magnified. A neutral look feels like rejection. A sigh feels like a verdict. A nothing-burger becomes a full meal of self-doubt. And you might not even realize what the stress is doing to you until a blowup happens.

We must control how we react to suboptimal situations.

Men are often taught to bury our feelings. If we admit we’re stressed, scared, or worried, we assume we’ll be seen as less capable. So we soldier on through bear markets, layoffs, and capital calls, and keep grinding. Most of us make it through. Some of us sadly don't. While others simply opt out of family formation altogether.

The same goes for any primary provider, regardless of gender. When the household depends on your income or your investment decisions, every bad outcome feels like your personal failure. And because you don’t want to worry anyone, you often carry it alone.

The problem is, stress doesn’t stay buried. It leaks out as irritability, sensitivity, and an inability to enjoy the moment you’re paying for.

If you’re the provider: say something. You don’t need to dump every number on your partner. But “I’m feeling stretched right now and might be more irritable than normal” goes a long way to set expectations. Silence forces your partner to guess, and they’ll often guess wrong.

If you’re the partner of a provider: know that the person who seems tense about a $1,200 hotel upgrade or a simple photo request may be carrying something heavier than they’re letting on. A little patience, a thank you, or a “how are you doing with everything?” can mean more than you’d think.

Since 2009, I’ve always told readers to save and invest until it hurts each month. Otherwise, you’re not saving enough. After 10 years of deliberate saving and investing, you’ll likely have far more than you imagined. Compounding sneaks up on you.

But I’ve always taken an extreme approach, and there’s a reason.

The summer after high school, a prank went wrong and I got in trouble with the law. I thought my life was over. I assumed no company would ever take a chance on me.

When one finally did, I swore I’d save and invest as much of every paycheck as possible so I’d never have to depend on someone accepting me again. I didn’t think many would.

Delaying gratification was painful yet comforting. Every dollar saved was a step toward never needing permission again. Luckily, the worst case scenario did not happen.

But now I have people depending on me who had nothing to do with my past mistakes. They shouldn’t have to live under the strain I put on myself. For the sake of harmony and happiness, I need to ease up.

From now on, I’m keeping at least six months of living expenses in cash or cash equivalents in my taxable brokerage account. No exceptions.

For years, holding cash felt wasteful because it earned next to nothing. But with money market funds and short-term Treasuries paying a respectable yield, the opportunity cost of sleeping well at night is much lower.

Cash isn’t just a return. It’s emotional capital. It’s what lets you say yes to a family trip without feeling like you’re stealing from your future. If you’re fully invested and a capital call, layoff, or market crash hits, you’re forced to make decisions from fear.

I’m a recovering optimizer. Saving $1,000 by cutting a night is fine. Spending the entire trip mentally tallying costs is not.

At some point, the marginal benefit of squeezing out another dollar is smaller than the cost to your relationships and your mood. Your kids won’t remember whether you got a great rate on the second room. They’ll remember whether Dad was present or distracted.

The portfolio: a happy family on vacation, kids laughing at rescue animals doing tricks, a jaw-dropping view at Red Rocks.

The positions: a photo angle, a lost poker hand, a capital call that will be met come hell or high water.

Any investor knows not to let one red position ruin a green portfolio. Yet I let one tiny position ruin an afternoon worth more than any return. Don’t be like me.

Once you hit middle age, it’s hard to change. It’s why so many couples split over irreconcilable differences. Both sides know what the other wants, both want to stay together, yet sustaining change is impossible.

But just like a near-death experience can make you stop taking life for granted, a stressful moment blown out of proportion can be a great catalyst for change. It shows you what’s actually going on beneath the surface.

I’m tired of optimizing every last dollar. Spending freely in Vegas for four days, minus that bomb pot, has loosened me up. And this change should make me a better husband, father, and personal finance writer.

Oh, and here’s one of the pictures my wife took of me during that moment. Turns out she knew exactly what she was doing all along.

Readers, have you ever felt like a burden to your loved ones, no matter how hard you try to provide? Has financial strain ever made you more sensitive to perceived slights? And for the partners out there, how do you support the provider in your household when you can tell they’re stressed?

You pay off your mortgages for “peace of mind”; I hoard cash equivalents (SGOV, PONAX, Short-term munis) for “peace of mind”. All my properties have a significant mortgage either through a traditional bank or my brokerage LOC. All are ARMs exposing me to interest rate fluctuations. As an apartment owner, I also have lawsuit risk, regulatory and statutory risk, natural disaster risk, etc. I don’t even count vacancies, non-payers and evictions anymore because those are certainties, not risks.

I also hoard credit card points; even if my investments tank, I will have a fund for inexpensive vacations. It’s a mental and emotional cushion when I’m getting a good deal on vacations even though I’m spending money. True. I set a budget of $500, and viewed it as entertainment and also as a chance to win. I have about an 80% winning record over the last 20 years.

It’s always good to review decisions and retrospect. Maybe I would’ve been happier if I had one $350. But I didn’t think I was unhappy or irritable or impatient to begin with that morning. Red rocks was really amazing.

Hi Sam Thats really good if you win 80% of the time How about we make a wager for charity? I will play you no limit poker. We both put up 10k and the proceeds go to the winners charity? You pick the spot Seems like a great opportunity for your charity? JJ

Could be fun! But you have to promise not to drink heavily and keep things pleasant. For our last bet of $5,000, some of your emails were unhinged after your lost. It’s important to keep things light and fun.

What’s the maximum you’re willing to bet? And would you be willing to fly to Honolulu? I’ll be there during the holidays for a couple weeks.

Sure Sam, too much alcohol is never good. I apologize for those comments. I am in the Cayman Islands over Christmas time. Pick another time, let’s keep it fun. I do appreciate what you do and look forward to your posts

So I would wager 21 k divided between 3 charities We could do it in Tahoe, Vegas, San Jose, Ventura, or Bristol

I remember a number of years ago I was stressed about money and we were driving home together since we worked together.So she says look at that homeless man standing on the corner. Then she says do you think he lost any money in the stock market today. So that puts it in perspective.

Good perspective. Always good to anppreciate what we have.

Although, it’s kind of nice not to have any money during a downturn.

I remember during the Global, financial crisis, my boss was trying to console me on my terrible bonus. And he said, “you should be happy you make so little. I’m getting crushed here making so much.”

I was attending an IT Cybersecurity conference with a couple of other senior partners when I got the call from the CEO. I had sold my company to them a couple of years prior and the company had recently lost a couple of major clients. They couldn’t afford to keep me on board anymore. I had equity in the company, but was also just another employee. There’s a longer back story, but I ended up staying for about another year at a severely reduced comp plan. It was an extremely stressful and difficult time even though on paper I had zero financial reason to keep working. I could have retired then, but my pride and ego would not allow it. The looming issue was we had a two week vacation planned for the Carolinas and then off to the Bahamas for a week on a sailboat. I was super stressed about the situation. They were going to lay me off, but wait! I have a big vacation planned the next month. As it turned out, the vacation was exactly what I needed and my family needed. I actually closed a deal at the airport on the way out, and then I was done with work for 2 weeks. Didn’t think about work again the entire time. Enjoy your time in Las Vegas with family. The money will always be there!

Everybody makes mistakes. Not Everyone admits them.

Thank you for trying to help us learn by yours.

OK that picture is fine! But you’re right…she was probably stressed too. Pick your battles. Let me tell you- I’ve been married for 35 years.

When you’re being photographed, you have no idea what the outcome is because you cannot see the picture after it is snapped. I just asked for a different angles given snapping is free.

The setting was majestical, so I didn’t take into consideration she could have been stressed. So it’s important to put myself in her shoes and not be quick to judge next time.

Happy to see this post Sam. After reading this I just added two extra days on my road trip and not going to worry about the extra money that will be spent. I am going to enjoy it and not fret over a couple thousand dollars. Thanks.

I LOVE the shirt….great post. Hang in there Sam, sounds like you’re human and continuing to learn everyday. Cheers!!

I love it too, which is why I thought it would be a fun profile pic. It’s so true as a parent to young children :)

Sam, another fantastic middle-age point of view and just full of common sense. I would add a 4th point for a middle-age financial provider, and that is especially if you have enjoyed some investment success is to stop trying to hit home runs and be satisfied with double, triples, and even some singles. What a great picture of you, thx for sharing and thx for listening.

Great article Great photo! Thanks for sharing!!

Vegas! So glad you went together. Even though it’s known as an adult destination there’s actually tons of great activities to do with kids there. And that’s great you also got to do an excursion to mix things up. There’s so much surrounding beauty and Red Rocks is quite an incredible place. It’s also so cool to see lots of rock climbers there. Great pic too!

Sam, I think you’re being awfully hard on yourself. I also think what you are feeling is very normal. Imagine being stretched ALL the time! That bit of anxiety, noticing how much every single thing costs, annoyed at gas prices, annoyed when kids ask for things for the 10th time that day, annoyed when the wife suggests we get take out for $100 after a busy week. “The silent burden of the primary provider”. This is very real for me; especially now after taking a medical retirement. You elude to this, but we have to realize we’ll be ok and that all our hard work and aggressive investing over the last several decades is exactly what these moments are for. Us type A personalities have a hard time chilling out, it’s how we’re built but it’s also how we got our successes and ultimately how we provide.

Life is interesting, isn’t it? Why do we feel the way we feel? And what can we recognize about ourselves to change to make things better for others.

Introspection can reveal a great deal if we let it happen.

#38. 11 Retirement Planning Mistakes That Haunt High-Earning Physicians

The scariest thing on a physician’s desk this October is the fourth-quarter estimated tax worksheet, propped against a 403(b) statement that hasn’t moved since spring.

Most retirement articles are written for someone worried about running out of money. You should worry about that too. On top of it, you carry a problem the average saver never meets: a tax code that takes 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700, trims your itemized deductions once you get there, shrinks your SALT break somewhere past $505,000, and reaches two years backward to set your Medicare premiums.

Every mistake on this list costs a little more in that bracket.

This list is built for physicians with six figures before the comma, including those who collect some or all of it on a 1099.

Physicians are one of the few groups positioned to collect the maximum Social Security benefit, because most of you clear the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December. That makes claiming age a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month; the same worker gets $4,152 at full retirement age and roughly $5,181 by holding out until 70. Claiming early trims the benefit permanently (5/9 of 1% per month for the first 36 months, 5/12 of 1% per month beyond that), and every year you wait past full retirement age adds 8%.

Dr. Addams claimed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums shifts at $200 an hour. Before full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480, so his own paycheck ate his benefit. (Social Security credits some of that back at full retirement age, but the cash-flow plan he built was toast.) Semi-retired physicians are exactly the people who keep earning after they file.

Two other quirks hit doctors harder. The formula averages your 35 highest-earning years, and residency plus a late start can leave early retirees with zeros in that average; the bend points in the formula soften the blow for high earners, but pull your record at ssa.gov before assuming anything.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a price no insurer will match.

A serious diagnosis or a family tree with short branches can justify claiming early. For a healthy 62-year-old internist with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

The textbook move as retirement approaches is to dial down risk. Physicians who take that advice too far end up with a portfolio that can’t outrun their withdrawals.

Run the timeline. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years or longer. A bond-heavy portfolio feels safe in year one and starts losing ground to inflation and withdrawals by year ten, which is why stocks still have to do some of the lifting deep into retirement.

High earners face a sneakier version of this mistake, and it lives in asset location. Taxable bond interest gets hit at ordinary rates. At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (which applies above $250,000 of modified AGI for married couples and has never been indexed for inflation), you hand close to 41 cents of every interest dollar to Washington before your state takes its cut.

Park bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b), hold broad stock index funds in taxable, and look at municipal bonds if you need fixed income outside retirement accounts.

How much stock is enough? That depends on your spending, your other income, and how well you sleep through a 25% drawdown. “As little as possible” is not an allocation.

Landmark Wealth Management puts the S&P 500’s annualized return from 1926 through 2024 at about 10.3%. It’s a lovely number, and nobody in history has received it in a straight line.

Sequence-of-returns risk turns a reasonable plan into a slasher film.

Two physicians retire with the same $4 million and the same 10-year average return. Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (who, it turns out, was not) retires into a bear market, sells shares near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back when prices recover. Same average, very different endings.

The 4% rule tries to account for that. William Bengen published it in 1994: withdraw 4% in year one, then adjust that dollar amount for inflation every year after. Bengen has since revised his own number upward to about 4.7%.

The real mistake is treating any single figure as permanent. Retirees who trim spending after bad years (guardrail strategies) or who keep two to three years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds (the bucket approach) give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Pick a method, stress-test it against a crash in year one, and expect to adjust it.

Read: Is the 4% Rule Too Frugal for Doctors?

Maxing your 401(k), 403(b), and 457(b) during peak earning years at 37% is a good move. The trouble starts when it’s the only move for 25 years.

Dr. Smart retires at 60 with $5 million, nearly all of it pre-tax. Required minimum distributions begin at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security, up to 85% of which is taxable.

Suddenly, a retired doctor is back in a high bracket, paying tax on money she deferred at a high bracket. Then Medicare notices.

Medicare’s IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at a modified AGI of $218,000 for couples ($109,000 single).

At the top tier, Part B jumps from the standard $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, which adds up to roughly $6,900 a year per person in surcharges alone. Medicare also uses a two-year look-back, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

The fix lives in the gap years. Retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade where taxable income is the lowest it’s been since residency. Converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth in that window, filling the lower brackets on purpose, shrinks future RMDs before they become a problem.

During your working years, fund backdoor Roth IRAs ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan.

If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already made that choice for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions have to go in as Roth.

Rental income, a part-time medical director role, or expert witness work can also give you an income stream that doesn’t depend on draining one enormous tax-deferred account.

Physicians tend to underestimate retirement spending for a simple reason: they’ve never tracked it. The paycheck covered everything, so nobody looked.

Pull 12 months of actual spending from your cards and accounts, then adjust for what changes after medicine. Disability insurance, licensing fees, CME, and the commute fall away. Travel tends to swell and front-load into the first decade.

Healthcare before Medicare can run five figures a year for a couple buying their own coverage. Long-term care waits at the back of the line: Genworth figures cited in Fisher Investments’ healthcare guide put a semi-private nursing home room at roughly $111,000 a year in 2024, and federal estimates say almost 70% of people will need some form of long-term care, for about three years on average.

Errors cut in two directions. Underestimate spending, and you drain the portfolio early. Overestimate it, and you work three extra years you didn’t need, a loss that never shows up on any statement.

Anyone who practiced through 2022 watched CPI peak at 9.1% that June. Inflation cooled afterward, but prices never went back down.

The damage compounds quietly. A $200,000 annual retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation. Any income stream that doesn’t adjust (a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, a practice buyout paid in level installments) loses purchasing power every year you hold it.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician payment has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 once you adjust for inflation in practice costs. Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched happen to your fee schedule, and build in an inflation assumption a bit above whatever the current forecast says.

The urge to leave is real, and it’s showing up earlier. In Doximity’s physician polling, the share of doctors aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement rose between 2023 and 2026, from 30% to 46%. Among emergency physicians, the figure climbed from 30% to 52%.

Burnout is a legitimate reason to change your life and a poor reason to skip the math. Retiring at 52 instead of 60 means eight fewer years of contributions, eight extra years of withdrawals, and a longer stretch buying your own health insurance before Medicare.

Several costs belong to medicine alone. If your malpractice policy is claims-made, leaving can trigger a tail coverage bill, often priced at a multiple of your annual premium, unless your employer covers it or your carrier offers a free tail at retirement age.

A few years away can complicate credentialing if you want back in, and some boards will ask for a formal re-entry program.

On the brighter side, physicians have unusual access to early withdrawals: governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age, and the rule of 55 lets you tap the 401(k) or 403(b) of the employer you leave in or after the year you turn 55.

A middle path often beats a hard stop. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or moving into a nonclinical role keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow a few more years untouched.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger number, and a market dip convinces you to stay another year, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve thought about slowing down.

Dr. Addams (yes, him again) planned to retire at 62, then 64, then “once the kids finish school.” His youngest graduated in 2019. Money saved after you’ve crossed the finish line buys very little extra safety, and the years spent earning it come out of your healthiest stretch of life.

Hospitals are changing the math as well. Some now require cognitive and physical screening for late-career physicians past a set age, so the decision to keep practicing may not stay entirely yours.

Pick a number and a date, and write down what you’ll do the Monday after. In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those who are simply running from the pager.

This is the first of three entries that replace the generic advice, and it’s the one high earners ask me about most.

Long-term rentals generate depreciation, but for a full-time physician those losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income.

Short-term rentals play by different rules. If the average guest stay is seven days or less, the property isn’t treated as a rental activity under the regulations. Materially participate (most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more hours than any other individual) and the losses become non-passive, free to offset your W-2 or 1099 income.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, permanently restored by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for property acquired after January 19, 2025, and the first-year numbers get large.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, depending on the property and the study. In the 37% bracket, that’s roughly $55,000 to $74,000 of federal tax that stays in your pocket.

The fine print, which the Instagram gurus skip, matters as much as the pitch:

If any of your income arrives on a 1099 (locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work, consulting), you have access to retirement accounts your W-2 colleagues can only envy.

Plenty of contractors open a SEP-IRA and stop there, which is an expensive default.

A Solo 401(k) usually beats it. For 2026, you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (a limit shared with any W-2 401(k) or 403(b) you also contribute to), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings as a sole proprietor, or 25% of W-2 salary through an S corporation, up to a combined $72,000.

Add $8,000 in catch-up contributions at 50, or $11,250 between ages 60 and 63. The employer side stands apart from your hospital plan, so an employed doc with meaningful side income can layer it on top of what they already contribute at work. The SEP has one more flaw for high earners: its balance counts under the pro-rata rule and sabotages the backdoor Roth.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan. It’s a defined benefit plan layered on top of the Solo 401(k), and allowable contributions rise with age, often into six figures a year for physicians in their 50s.

You’ll need an actuary and a funding commitment you can’t skip in a lean year, so it suits consistent earners.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Those deductions do double duty because of the QBI cliff. Physicians run a “specified service trade or business,” so the 20% qualified business income deduction phases out as taxable income rises.

For 2026, married couples get the full deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it vanishes entirely at $553,500 (the single thresholds are $201,750 and $276,750).

Dr. Lucky, married with roughly $500,000 of taxable 1099 income, sits deep in the phase-out. Fund the Solo 401(k) and a cash balance plan, drop taxable income below $403,500, and the QBI deduction rises from the dead on top of the retirement deduction itself.

Self-employment tax deserves a sentence of its own. Contractors pay the employee and employer shares of Social Security (12.4% combined) up to the $184,500 wage base and 2.9% Medicare on everything, plus another 0.9% above $250,000 for married couples.

An S corporation paying you a reasonable salary can trim part of that, though it adds payroll, a separate return, and a salary figure the IRS will scrutinize.

Physicians start saving late. Residency ends somewhere around 30 or 32, often with six-figure student debt, so the compounding years most savers get in their 20s went to call rooms and loan servicers. A year-end cram session can’t make that up.

The calendar matters more than usual this fall. These items won’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

Pick one item from this list before you hand out the first fun-size Snickers, and make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

Great insights here! It’s fascinating how these retirement planning mistakes can ripple into broader financial security issues. On a lighter note, I often play quordle game to keep my mind sharp while strategizing my finances. Balancing fun and financial planning makes it all feel less daunting!

TL;DR: Falling Treasury yields are taking mortgage rates down with them.

Mortgage rates are starting off this week with a nice drop, though the likely reason for the fall could be a little anxiety-inducing.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.20% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 15 basis points lower than Friday and 12 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

Rates started this slide last week, as investors' previously sky-high confidence in AI came a little closer to earth. Tech stocks lost a bit of their luster, and bonds looked more appealing. Greater demand for bonds pushed up bond prices, dropping bond yields (they move inversely). And mortgage rates are often indexed to the yield on the 10-year Treasury so, huzzah, lower mortgage rates.

On one hand, yay! But on the other hand … uh, what was that about stocks? For way more detail, keep reading below the chart.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, mortgage rates started edging lower last week as Treasury yields came down. Mortgage rates are generally benchmarked to the yield on 10-year Treasury notes, so where the yield goes, rates go, too.

The yield is basically the return investors get on a bond. A bond is a little piece of government or corporate debt; when an investor buys a bond, they're making a tiny loan to the issuer. The issuer agrees to pay them back a set amount over the bond's lifespan (that's the yield), and when the bond matures, the investor gets the bond's original price back. That's why unlike anything-could-happen stocks, bonds are generally considered relatively low risk.

A bond investor who buys a bond at issuance knows immediately: Here's my cost, here's what I'll earn and here's when my initial investment will be returned. When investors sell bonds to each other, things get more interesting, because the market now determines the price, and that shifts the relative value of the yield.

Here's how that works. If you bought a $100 bond with $5 annual yield payments, that yield is 5%. But say you want to sell that bond but can’t find a full-price buyer; the best price you can get for it is $80. The annual yield payments are still $5, but since they're relative to that lower price, the yield is now 6.25%.

For much of the summer and early fall, we saw lots of Treasury bond selling, which drove prices down and yields up. That kept pushing mortgage rates higher. Additionally, tech companies issuing loads of corporate bonds to help fund AI buildout meant that bond investors had a sexier option than Plain Jane Treasuries.

Last week, that dynamic reversed as doubts crept in about the potential profits from AI. September's Consumer Price Index, which came out last Wednesday, and Producer Price Index, from Thursday, showed that inflation's still running hot. If prices are climbing, the costs of building data structures and other AI infrastructure will increase, right? So to get solid returns on these investments, tech companies are going to have to make some serious profits. That right there is where some investors are having misgivings.

It sort of played out like a teen movie. Investors realized that the hot, popular girl (tech stocks) might not actually be all that, and their eyes turned to the reliable girl-next-door who'd been there for them all along (Treasuries).

Just so we're clear: No one is saying the AI bubble is bursting, or really that there even is an AI bubble. But yes, prices for Treasuries went up and yields fell, so mortgage rates ebbed, too. Whether this downward trend will last depends on a lot of factors, including whether tech companies can convince investors that they're on track for strong profits and whether anything can improve fuel prices, since that's a massive factor in inflation.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.70% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#44. What Are Target Date Funds?

Some products in this article are from our partners. Read our Advertiser Discloser.

When you sign up for a 401(k) at work, there is a good chance that a target date fund shows up near the top of the investment options list. They are simple, widely available, and often the default choice for new investors. But simple does not always mean the best option for your situation.

In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.

A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund that most closely matches the year you plan to retire, and the fund handles everything else. If you plan to retire around 2050, for example, you would choose a fund labeled something like “2050 Retirement Fund” or “Target Date 2050.”

The fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer. Early on, the fund is weighted heavily toward growth stocks. As retirement approaches, the portfolio gradually shifts toward bonds and more conservative holdings to reduce risk.

The appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly, and the fund adjusts itself. For people who want to set it and forget it, that sounds like a dream. But there is more to the story.

Target date funds are known as “fund of funds.” Rather than holding individual stocks or bonds directly, they hold a collection of other mutual funds, typically a mix of domestic stock, international stock, and bond funds.

The fund manager adjusts the allocation over time according to a schedule called a glide path. When you are decades away from retirement, the fund might hold 90% stocks and 10% bonds. As you get closer to your target year, that ratio shifts until the fund is much more conservative, sometimes holding more bonds than stocks by the time you retire.

This rebalancing happens automatically inside the fund, which is one reason they are so popular in workplace retirement plans. You do not need to log in and make adjustments. The fund does it for you.

The glide path is simply the schedule that determines how the fund’s asset allocation changes over time. Think of it as the fund’s long-term plan for gradually reducing risk.

Different fund providers use different glide paths, and this matters more than most people realize. Some funds are more aggressive early on and pull back dramatically as retirement nears. Others maintain a higher stock allocation even into and through retirement, which some financial planners argue is actually smarter given how long retirement can last.

The important thing to understand is that the glide path is not customized for you. It is a one-size-fits-all formula based on your expected retirement year, nothing more. Your actual risk tolerance, health, spending plans, and other income sources are not factored in at all.

The biggest selling point is that target date funds require almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly, and walk away. For someone who has no interest in managing their investments, that convenience is genuinely valuable.

Because target date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds, you get broad diversification across asset classes in a single investment. You are not putting all your money into a single sector or company.

Over time, a portfolio can drift away from its intended allocation as different assets grow at different rates. Target date funds handle this automatically, which is one less thing you have to manage yourself.

Target date funds are not without their drawbacks, and for many investors, those drawbacks are significant enough to look for a better option.

Because target date funds are funds of funds, they often carry two layers of fees: the expense ratio of the target date fund itself and the underlying expense ratios of the funds it holds. Even a seemingly small difference in fees can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a long investing career. Low-cost index funds, by comparison, often charge a fraction of what target date funds do.

The glide path in a target-date fund is designed for the average investor retiring in a given year. But your situation is not average. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income, or a much higher risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that is reflected in how the fund manages your money.

When you hand everything over to a target date fund, you give up control over your allocation. If the fund has a heavy position in international stocks or bonds that you would rather avoid, there is not much you can do about it while staying in the fund.

Not all target date funds are created equal. The same target year fund from two different providers can have very different allocations, fee structures, and underlying holdings. Without digging into the details, it is easy to end up in a fund that does not match your actual needs.

This is where the comparison gets important. A target date fund is actively managed in the sense that a team of people decides how to allocate and rebalance it over time. An index fund, on the other hand, simply tracks a market index like the S&P 500. There is no active management involved, which is exactly why the fees are so much lower.

Decades of research consistently show that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after fees. Target date funds are not immune to this problem. When you account for layered costs, many target-date funds trail what you would earn by simply holding a low-cost index fund over the same period.

A simple alternative that many investors use is called a three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total market index fund, an international index fund, and a bond index fund. You set your own allocation based on your age and risk tolerance, rebalance once a year, and pay minimal fees. It takes about 30 minutes a year to manage.

This approach gives you the same diversification as a target-date fund, with far more control and significantly lower costs. And as a general rule, the more of your return you keep rather than paying in fees, the better off you will be over time.

Target date funds are not the right choice for every investor, but there are situations where they make sense.

Even in these cases, it is worth checking the expense ratio. If your plan offers a target-date fund with an expense ratio above 0.50%, consider whether there are lower-cost index fund options within the same plan.

Target date funds solve a real problem: they make it easy for people who do not want to think about investing to still participate in the market. That convenience has real value.

But for investors who are willing to learn even a little bit about how to manage their own allocation, a portfolio of low-cost index funds will almost always be the better long-term choice. The fees are lower, the control is greater, and the returns tend to be better over time.

If you are currently in a target date fund, that is not necessarily a problem. But it is worth understanding what you are paying and whether a simpler, lower-cost approach might serve you better. Investing at least 10% of your gross income is the priority. Where exactly that money goes is the next question worth asking.

#45. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re currently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

As I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country.  They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a company in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most important part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to plan far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.)

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some new models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

But in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This big picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

But when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

So right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:

Even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

So in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re quickly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The most important phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:

I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald announced his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines

Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

So as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Why We Are Not Really All Doomed – the original all-purpose MMM article which explains why we never really have to worry about the long-term economic future.

There’s one more possible reason for the tariffs that you didn’t mention: Trump might be running a giant pump-and-dump scheme on the entire U.S. economy.

It’s very possible that he’s tipping off his pals right before he announces new tariffs, so they can buy at a bargain when the stock market drops. Then, when they want to sell, he cancels the tariffs so the market bounces back up. It wouldn’t be any more outrageous or corrupt than some of the other things he’s doing openly.

Of course, Mustachians who don’t overreact to the news aren’t affected by this! This is why long-term buy-and-hold is the right strategy, even when we have a tinpot tyrant with delusions of royalty at the helm.

Quite possibly: covered by @unusual_whales on X, a lot of people have made a lot of money….

Can we get on the Signal chat where the president tips off his cronies? I’d move away from long-term buy-and-hold if I knew when the market was about to react to tariff news…

One more possible reason goes somewhat into a similar direction.

I believe it could be verified with data from https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/schedules-federal-debt-daily/daily-activity (looks like a reliable source to me?) but I have not managed to get it working with this instruction here: https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/api-documentation/ :( so please take this with a grain of salt

First of all, most of the tariffs (or threatened tariffs) haven’t even hit yet.

Consumers will also react to rising prices by scaling back their spending, which shifts prices back down the supply/demand curve a little.

In the extreme case, high tariffs can even cause a recession which lowers demand for almost all goods and services, which means that prices for domestically produced services with elastic pricing might go down and bring the overall inflation numbers back in check.
