Might be semantic, but maybe tariffs are not “inflation”. It would be like saying that a VAT would be inflationary. Instead, this is a one-time step-function change in the cost of goods, then inflation (velocity) resumes on the new cost base. Oren Cass had an interesting blog article on this last week. At least food for thought – he posits that economists don’t actually think tariffs are inflationary.

100% the case. Inflation is caused by an increase in the money supply, by definition. It means your purchasing power is worth less. A one-time increase in a specific category of goods of 15% is not “inflation.” Meanwhile, every time the government uses printed (or digitally entered) dollars to spend trillions they don’t have, inflation grows massively and compounds, and for some reason, the majority of people don’t bat an eye.

A great analogy for inflation would be something like this… You are in charge of the county fair. There are a bunch of vendors of popcorn, cotton candy, and ride like ferris wheels, etc. You print tickets that visitors can use to acquire these goods and ride these rides, and the vendors set their own ticket prices. You and your friends discover you can give yourselves tickets and get more popcorn and ride more rides since you own the ticket machine. With the flood of tickets, the vendors realize they can (and need to) raise their prices. This is inflation. And it doesn’t matter if it’s due to your and your friends doing it for yourselves, or just doing it because of more guests coming to the fair (for “growth”).

I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply. Money supply is one factor in that, but so is the overall supply and demand of everything that is for sale. Money supply is increased or decreased as needed in reaction to what’s happening with prices, in order to keep prices more stable, if the system is well managed.

In your county fair example, you are holding the number of vendors and the items and quantities for sale as a constant while increasing the number of tickets. In reality the fair’s mini-economy will grow and shrink over time, and if the ticket supply were forced to always stay constant the ticket prices of rides, popcorn and cotton candy would move up and down significantly in reaction.

“I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply.”

Well, that’s the problem – that is wrong. A rise in prices is a symptom of inflation. It is not inflation nor is it the cause of inflation. Inflation is similar in concept to dilution.

No it’s not wrong. Inflation is prices going higher as time passes. The causes of inflation are debatable, but “inflation” is a word that refers to prices going up regardless of the cause.

It’s possible for money supply to increase without inflation. Japanese deflation and lost decades are a prime example.

But, yet, the employment reports show low unemployment, and jobs added with each passing month. What gives?

I believe that the answer lies in the gig economy and with self-employed workers. There are some 50 million Americans working gig work, self-employed, or who work as contractors. However, when that work becomes harder and harder, and it is no longer feasible to support yourself or your family on your combined uber, amazon delivery, lyft, and doordash routine, you begin to take that unappealing job for $45K per year.

But the employment report shows it as a net positive.

I believe that this effect does two things:

Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

This is an interesting analysis. The way I summed it up to an acquaintance is that Trump is playing with fire. In the end, it may be that we have something nice and shiny as a result. However, it is just as likely (if not more) that this whole thing is a dumpster fire and in the end it will just a smoking heap of ash.

However, the more fundamental problem here is that the reason that things like this (i.e., Trump unilaterally going tariff-nuclear, which is actually quite similar to what Biden did trying to illegally wipe out student loan debt, it’s just that Trump’s actions are at a different order of magnitude) is because Congress actively refuses to do their jobs. In the last several decades they have rather been rather determined to pass really loose/broad laws and specifically leave the “details” to the executive branch (either as some nebulous presidential power, or via some rule-making provision for an executive agency). This was bad but not terrible as long as we were electing presidents who were within a standard deviation of the ‘center’ of the political spectrum. However, Trump is a major outlier, and now it is readily apparent that Congress’ approach of letting the executive branch decide most things for itself isn’t actually a really good idea.

Even going back to the difference between Trump’s use of tariffs and Biden’s student debt cancellation efforts, it is clear that Biden’s policy, while objectively of very dubious legality, didn’t move the macroeconomic needle. Trump’s policies, on the other hand, even if they turn out to be completely legal (which I’m not sure they will), are rather painful object lesson on why Congress needs to actually do their jobs with a bit more effort.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

I think that there is a case to be made that sales taxes, above all other taxes, are the most “just” taxes. The idea is that sales taxes are the form of taxes that give the individual tax payer the greatest degree of economic freedom. Don’t want to pay so much in taxes? Then just buy less stuff!

This sort of thing is very difficult with other forms of taxes, because there aren’t reasonable ways to reduce property taxes, and in some cases (i.e., gentrification) your taxes can increase by huge amounts even if you do nothing at all but sit at home. Income taxes, excise taxes, and tariffs live in a bit of a middle ground (they provide a bit more economic freedom, but are still more difficult than sales taxes to deal with in terms of accomplishing the “I want to pay less tax” objective).

I disagree with the word “regressive.” It oversimplifies and is biased language. The thing is, the phenomenon you’re describing is simply an effect of a person being rich. The same percentage added to the sale of a good treats everyone equally – the difference is one person is rich. It’s not “hurting” the poorer person, it’s just that the rich person has a lot of money…because they’re rich. And when it comes to income taxes, “progressive” taxation is not more fair, it’s less fair. A percentage is already “progressive” because of math – 10% of $100,000 is $10,000 and 10% of $1 million is $100,000 – 10 times more tax revenue for 10 times the income. That’s completely fair. The idea of confiscating an escalating percentage is not more fair.

The math changes if you consider the marginal value of a dollar to someone who is rich vs someone who is poor. A thousand dollars more or less to someone making minimum wage is significant when measured in how much it will impact their lives. A thousand dollars more or less to a multi-millionaire with a high six figure income is barely noticeable. I agree that a simple percentage tax is more “fair” if what you’re measuring is dollars, but I think it’s less “fair” if what you’re measuring is impact on someone’s life. That said, lowering taxes helps everyone.

That’s the whole point of earning more: the marginal value changes and you can afford more. Taxes are the same as groceries, or your house bills, or anything else. Money is fungible. By raising the tax rate on higher levels of income, you’re just advocating for redistribution of wealth.

It’s true that money is fungible in terms of what it will buy, but it’s not fungible in terms of life impact. Take $5K from someone who is barely scraping by and they might lose the roof over their head. Take $50K from someone wealthy and they will (justifiably!) be annoyed but it won’t put them on the street. In this case the $5K is more life changing than the $50K. I’d say I’m advocating for a tax regime that provides “more even distribution of pain (via lived experience)” rather than anything else, while still keeping taxes low enough overall to minimize disincentives for earning and building wealth. As you note below a “zero tax for people earning below a certain amount” does this and seems reasonable to me.

With all due respect, you, and unfortunately, many others, are missing the point.

We (and Trump) get that the cost will get passed onto the consumers. Or at least that’s the “first order effect” (to borrow your phrase.)

What you’re missing is that consumers get to decide between whether to purchase the item or not. If they are willing to eat the cost, and the item is something they absolutely can’t live without, they’ll buy it. Or they won’t buy it at all.

In the latter case, the sales numbers (and thus revenue) of the company selling the goods will drop. At which point that company has a choice to make: live with the drop in sales, and thus bottom line, eat part of the tariff or all of it, in order to increase volume.

Obviously, the company’s goal (let’s use Nike as an example), is to make as much money as possible. So if they naively pass 100% of the cost onto the consumer, their sales might drop so much that they’ll realize that wasn’t the best financial decision. This is an optimization problem: find the global maximum. The variables are: what % of tariffs to eat (vs pass on), whether to continue to offshore or onshore (and to what degree), and so on.

Using the Nike example (because they recently sobbed about their $1Bn tariff bill), their product is, among other things, athletic shoes. They’re not an essential item. They’re a luxury. It’s also not something you buy every week. Consumers can easily forego purchasing a new pair of Nike shoes, and Nike can decide if it can stomach the sales drop or not and react accordingly. That’s not our concern. We shouldn’t feel sorry for Nike who got rich at the expense of exploiting sweat job labor and pocketing the enormous margins, while selling out American jobs.

The other second-order effect you missed is the fact that by creating these “tariff walls” the money stays onshore. I.e. customers buy US-made goods and pay local companies, i.e. their fellow citizen. The money feeds back into the US economy. Without them, even though goods are “cheaper” for the consumer, the money flows out of the country: enriching China and other third world countries at our expense. What are some third-order effects you think might arise from that? I hope you see how this thinking is a bit short-sighted.

Of course, if one’s goals are not to support and protect the USA and its people, then the above will seem silly and pointless (or even absurd!). A trade deficit means that the other countries are receiving more money than they are paying. But what do they then do with it? So the central banks of the other countries are amassing an immense amount of dollars which they are not spending on buying US products due to the trade deficit. And judging from data from these central banks, they seem to be doing mainly one thing with these. Buying US treasury bonds. Which I find interesting, because these bonds will return more dollars which they then spend on buying more bonds because the US is not producing enough interesting-to-them goods or services to trade these dollars for.

Sounds like actually a good system from US perspective to me? Buy stuff from the other countries for dollars and they will give these dollars back in the form of US treasury bonds that can be used by the US government to then again spend within the US, for building infrastructure or paying social security.

And we all know how the US treasury bonds will be paid back when they come due. By selling more US treasury bonds. Which seem to be in good demand as the central banks of all the other countries want to put their dollars to use in some way.

I think I once heard a saying: If you owe 2 million dollars to the bank, the bank owns you. If you owe 2 trillion dollars, you own the bank.

Replace “you” by “US” and “bank” by “other countries” in that and the whole situation looks actually quite good from an US perspective to me. So looking back, should one really be surprised of what Nixon did in 1971 ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock )? I mean, why would the others buy treasury bonds that only give them back more dollars when they could trade the dollars they buy the bonds with for gold?

#46. Manifesting Money When You Have None: It’s Worth A Try

At some point, you might find yourself short on money with no obvious way to fix it. You'll have a plan. You'll have strategies. But you won't know exactly where the money will come from.

That's where I am right now. So I tried something that might make some of you groan: I manifested money.

You've probably done it too, even if you didn't call it that. People manifest their destiny all the time by telling themselves what they want or deserve:

I want to find a girlfriend or boyfriend.

I will get promoted to managing director.

I will lose 10 pounds this year and keep it off for the rest of my life.

I will perform in front of a large crowd and make no mistakes.

Some of these come true. Many do not, but they are still worth trying.

So I figured, if people can manifest a spouse or a promotion, why not money? There's no harm in thinking about money coming to you in the least expected ways.

Before you click away, hear me out. This isn't my first manifestation rodeo. The last time I did it, I left a finance career six years earlier than planned.

I've been cash poor lately because of aggressive capital calls. I budgeted for up to $300,000 in capital calls over the first 12 months of a $1 million venture fund commitment. Within six months, $460,000 had been called.

That's a $160,000 hole, in half the time.

The good news is our passive income still covers all our living expenses. The bad news is that if another capital call hits in the next couple of months, I won't have the funds.

One morning I was sitting in the hot tub, thinking about what to write next on Financial Samurai. Out of nowhere I started saying, “Let the money come in unexpected ways.”

I said it a couple of times. Then I went back to scrolling the news on my phone. Very spiritual.

A week later, I went to my PO Box to mail a signed copy of Millionaire Milestones to a consulting client. Every client gets a signed copy of a first print, first edition, which could one day be worth a lot more if you enjoy collecting books. I hadn't checked my mailbox in three weeks, so mail had piled up.

One envelope was from the tax authorities. That always makes my heart skip a beat.

But this time there was a check inside for $2,799. Yeah baby yeah!

It turns out that on my April 15 extension filing, I reported zero estimated tax payments when I had actually made some. Then when I filed my full return in September, I paid California another $650, based on what the tax software told me to pay. So the Franchise Tax Board sent back money I didn't know I was owed.

Technically it was my money all along, returned because of my own carelessness. But it felt like free money, and I desperately needed it to rebuild my cash buffer.

It gets better. The federal government apparently owes me a refund too according to a letter they sent, but couldn't pay it because I'd never added my bank account to my IRS online account. I didn't even know that option existed. I logged on, added my checking account, and I'm now waiting for another surprise.

The second surprise was consulting demand. I don't advertise my financial consulting, because demand can be overwhelming and each session takes a lot of work. I prefer about one or two a month.

After the hot tub session, within a week, four people reached out. I said yes to all of them and spaced them out to one per week. That built another 1% buffer for future capital calls.

Although one client still hasn't paid after nine days. Further, I forgot to ask for a deposit because I confused another deposit for theirs given the sudden flurry of demand. Apparently the universe delivers the leads but not accounts receivable.

The third surprise was a $1,758.65 distribution from a private real estate fund I invested in almost 10 years ago. The fund has already paid back all my capital and then some, so it’s been off my radar. Out of 17 assets, it has four remaining ones, three of which are performing OK. The last distribution was at least six months ago. $1,758.65 isn't much, but every dollar counts.

The fourth surprise was found money of a different kind.

I was going through one of our 40+ financial accounts and noticed an investment that had underperformed for four years. I hadn't noticed it earlier because it's held in our corporate account, which my wife mainly overseas.

I didn't think it would recover in the next 12 months, so I sold it at no capital gain, sad, I know. My original plan was too hold it for 10 years, and I still have $165,000 remaining. But that one sale created a buffer for a 13.7% capital call, or $137,000.

I was thrilled because I had not counted this position in my net worth at all. Hooray for having separate accounts and not being able to keep track of everything well.

The fifth manifestation surprise came from my inbox. The chief marketing officer of a former affiliate partner emailed me out of the blue. We worked together for several years about a decade ago, and then life moved on.

He's joined a new firm whose product automates banking and bookkeeping for real estate investors. As a landlord who still tracks rent and repairs with a mix of spreadsheets and denial, I get the appeal. It could be a good fit for the Financial Samurai community, but I'll do my due diligence before saying yes.

Even if nothing comes of it, the lesson stands: relationships you built 10 years ago can still pay off. Treat people well because you never know who'll come back around.

For perspective, I have not gone prospecting for online business for years. Instead, I just field inbound inquires and decline 99% of them.

All told, I now have about $18,000 in my personal accounts and $137,000 in our corporate account, ready for the next series of capital calls. Any federal tax refund or new partnership income is gravy. That should buy me three to six months of breathing room. Meanwhile, I'll keep building cash from cash flow.

This isn't the first time manifesting has bailed me out.

In 1999, I started my career in New York City. Being at the office by 5:30am was expected. One morning, walking in before sunrise, it hit me: there was no way I could do this for three or four decades.

So I manifested my destiny. I'd be out of finance by 40.

I didn't just say it once. That goal became the filter for every financial decision I made for the next 13 years. I saved and invested 50% to 80% of my after-tax income and 98% of my bonus every year. The sacrifices required to achieve financial independence no longer felt like restrictions. Instead, every dollar saved felt one step closer to liberation.

When it was finally time to jump, I manifested a solution to the next problem: how to leave without walking away from five years of deferred compensation. Instead of quitting, I negotiated a severance. I kept all my deferred compensation, got a six-figure severance check, and left with a parachute and a buffer.

I left in 2012 at 34. Six years ahead of schedule.

If you're thinking about leaving a job you no longer love, don't quit. Quitting means walking away with nothing. Get laid off with a severance package instead.

I wrote How To Engineer Your Layoff to show you how I negotiated mine, and how you can do the same. You'll learn how to approach your manager, what you can ask for, and how to leave with a parachute instead of a pink slip and an empty bank account.

Thousands of readers have used it to buy time, a financial buffer, and a fresh start. Use the code “saveten” at checkout to save $10.

Here's what I've learned from both experiences. Manifesting isn't magic. It's direction.

Go back to that list at the top. The difference between the ones that come true and the ones that become annual traditions isn't how often you say them. It's whether saying them changes what you do the next morning.

When you say out loud what you want, you start noticing things you'd otherwise ignore. The PO Box and gym you've been avoiding. The government portal you didn't know existed. The underperforming position you've been too stubborn or too loyal to sell. The consulting requests you'd normally decline.

Every dollar I “manifested” this month was already mine or earned by me. Manifesting just made me go look.

The same was true in 1999. Wanting to retire early didn't save the money. Saving 50-80% of my income did. But without a clear destiny, I never would have had the discipline to keep doing it for 13 years.

So what does a good life actually look like to you?

Once you've got a good idea, here's how to make manifesting do something useful:

When your back is against the wall, you'll usually find a way out. Sometimes the solution has been sitting in your mailbox for four weeks.

Now, if I could just manifest four-pack abs, that would be an amazing feat. But you can't have everything.

Readers, have you ever manifested money or a big life goal into reality, and did it come with a plan or just good vibes? What does a good life look like to you, and what's the one thing standing between you and it? Have you ever found money that was yours all along?

Systeme.io has burst onto the digital marketing scene, brandishing a bold claim as an all-in-one, free platform.

Let’s face it, when you hear something like that, your first thought is, “This has got to be too good to be true.”

That was my initial reaction too. A free, do-it-all software that doesn’t suck? Highly doubtful.

But here’s the shocker: Systeme.io isn’t just blowing smoke. It’s a game-changer. As someone who’s navigated the maze of digital marketing tools, I was prepared for disappointment. Yet, Systeme.io left me floored with its capabilities.

Take it from someone who’s been around the block with the likes of ConvertKit, AWeber, and MailChimp. These giants lure you in with free offerings, only to tighten the screws when your audience grows. Then there’s WordPress.org – great for setting up a blog, but it’s like climbing Everest if you’re a newbie.

Systeme.io, on the other hand, is a beast of a different nature. Offering highly effective landing pages and robust sales funnels with professional templates for free? That’s unheard of. It’s like stumbling upon a treasure chest in your backyard.

My first foray into landing page software was with ClickFunnels, an undeniably powerful tool. But once the 14-day trial evaporates, you’re staring down the barrel of a $100 monthly fee. Worth it if you’re a pro, but a gut punch for beginners.

Yes, you can test it out 100% completely FREE.

And when the time comes to open your wallet, it’s less than $30 a month – an absolute steal for the arsenal of tools you’re getting.

Absolutely. It’s a diamond in the rough, especially for those just starting their digital marketing journey. For the veterans, it might not have the same allure, but for the rookies, it’s a godsend. Forget the skepticism; Systeme.io is a disruptor that’s here to stay.

The platform serves a multifaceted purpose, aiming to simplify the digital marketing process. It’s designed for entrepreneurs and businesses seeking an integrated solution for email marketing, sales funnels, website building, and more.

The importance of such a tool lies in its ability to streamline various marketing tasks, which are often scattered across different platforms, into one cohesive system.

The user interface of Systeme.io? It’s okay, but let’s not sugarcoat it. For a newbie who’s never dabbled in sales funnels or email campaigns, it can feel like being thrown into the deep end. It’s not the sleek, intuitive experience that tech gurus might rave about. But, and this is a big but, Systeme.io doesn’t just leave you hanging.

The saving grace here is their tutorials. These are goldmines for beginners. They walk you through the process, breaking down what could be an overwhelming experience into manageable chunks. So, while the interface might not win any beauty contests, the support system in place is BIG help.

At the core of Systeme.io are several key features that make it a comprehensive digital marketing solution. These include email marketing capabilities, sales funnel creation tools, a website builder, options for hosting membership sites, and affiliate program management.

Each of these features is designed to work seamlessly with the others, providing a unified experience. For instance, the email marketing service is notably efficient, rivaling established providers like ConvertKit, AWeber, and MailChimp, especially with its free subscription model that remains functional up to a certain point.

Here’s a sample template they offer for their email campaigns:

Here’s a breakdown of all the features Systeme.io offers:

And if here’s a fancy table to help simplify it even more:

When we talk about the cost-effectiveness of Systeme.io, we’re looking at a platform that offers a substantial suite of features without the hefty price tag that usually accompanies such versatility.

For starters, Systeme.io’s freemium model is a standout in the digital marketing space (click here to open a free account today). You can manage up to 2,000 contacts and create three sales funnels without spending a penny. This is a significant advantage for entrepreneurs and small businesses where every dollar counts.

To put this into perspective, let’s compare it with some industry counterparts. Platforms like ClickFunnels and Kartra, while offering robust functionalities, start their pricing at around $97 to $99 per month after their trial periods. This can be a steep investment for those just starting out.

In contrast, Systeme.io not only allows you to test the waters for free but also keeps the costs low even when you upgrade. Their paid plans, offering a broader range of features, start at less than $30 a month.

This pricing strategy makes advanced digital marketing tools accessible to a wider audience, breaking down the financial barriers that often hinder small businesses and startups.

The all-in-one nature of Systeme.io is its hallmark. It consolidates various marketing tools into one cohesive platform. This integration means you can manage email campaigns, build sales funnels, create websites, and even run affiliate programs without having to switch between different software. For many users, this integration simplifies the digital marketing process significantly, allowing for a more streamlined workflow.

However, it’s important to recognize that while Systeme.io covers a broad spectrum of functionalities, it may not offer the same depth as specialized standalone tools in each specific area.

For instance, while its email marketing capabilities are robust, they might not have the advanced features of a dedicated email marketing service.

Similarly, its website builder is competent for basic to intermediate needs, but it might not satisfy users looking for highly advanced web design features.

Systeme.io aims to be user-friendly, and for the most part, it achieves this goal. The interface is designed to be intuitive, especially for those who have basic familiarity with digital marketing tools. However, for complete beginners, there can be a learning curve.

The platform offers a range of tutorials and support materials, which are invaluable for new users. I’ve watched (and rewatched) several of these tutorials to lean how to use their software.

These resources are designed to help users navigate through the initial complexity and make the most out of the platform’s features.

Let’s get real about customization in Systeme.io. It’s got a decent selection of templates and the interface won’t make you pull your hair out, but if you’re looking to really dive deep into customization, you might hit a wall.

For those who have grand visions of a highly unique and tailored digital presence, Systeme.io can feel a bit like playing with kid gloves. It’s great for getting you up and running, but for the more ambitious or specific design needs, it’s not quite the creative playground you might be looking for.

Now, onto scalability. Systeme.io is like that compact car that’s perfect for city driving but struggles a bit on the open highway. For small businesses or solo entrepreneurs just starting out, it’s a match made in heaven. But as your business grows and your needs become more complex, Systeme.io might start to feel a bit cramped.

This is especially true for larger businesses or those niche ventures that need more than just the basics. As you scale up, you might find yourself needing more sophisticated tools and features that Systeme.io doesn’t offer.

Plus, when it comes to playing nice with other tools or services you might be using, Systeme.io isn’t always the most cooperative. It works well within its own confines but doesn’t always reach out to others easily.

Here’s a quick rundown on the pros and cons of Systeme.io

When compared to competitors, Systeme.io’s pricing is highly competitive. For instance, platforms like ClickFunnels offer powerful functionality but at a higher cost, typically starting at around $100 per month after a free trial. This can be a significant investment, especially for new entrepreneurs or small businesses.

In contrast, Systeme.io’s paid plans, which provide access to a broader range of features, are more affordable, starting at less than $30 a month.

To provide a broader perspective, let’s compare Systeme.io with other popular tools in the market:

This comparison shows that while Systeme.io offers a comprehensive suite of tools at an affordable price, platforms like HubSpot and Kartra provide more advanced features in certain areas but at a higher cost. ClickFunnels, on the other hand, is more expensive but offers highly customizable funnel-building capabilities.

User reviews and testimonials play a crucial role in understanding the real-world effectiveness of Systeme.io. Many users have shared success stories, highlighting how the platform has helped them streamline their marketing efforts and grow their businesses.

Upon reviewing their Trustpilot account, you can see the experience with Systeme.io is remarkable. Currently, there are 3,635 reviews with an average rating of 4.9. That is outstanding!

However, it’s also important to consider critiques and common issues raised by users. Some have pointed out the limitations in customization and scalability, as mentioned earlier. These critiques are valuable for potential users to set realistic expectations and for the platform’s developers to identify areas for improvement.

I currently have accounts with Systeme.io, Click Funnels, and Kajabi. To show you how they compare here’s a look at 3 different landing pages I’ve created each of them.

When you factor in both Click Funnels and Kajabi only offer free trials (around 14 days) and you have to start paying after that, the Systeme.io funnel becomes THAT more attractive. Here’s a look at some of the templates they offer for free:

In essence, while Systeme.io is a fantastic starting point for new online businesses, offering a solid foundation and easy-to-use tools, it’s not the endgame for everyone.

As your business evolves, you might outgrow its capabilities and start looking for something that offers a bit more room to stretch your entrepreneurial legs.

It’s a great launchpad, but for those on a path to rapid growth or with highly specific needs, keep in mind that you might need to eventually graduate to more advanced tools.

#52. Personal Investments • Re: In retirement should the goal be just a Roth IRA?

As one actively converts assets from a traditional IRA to a Roth in retirement should the goal always be to exhaust the traditional completely and have just a Roth? Just for round numbers, if the traditional started at 500K and you did conversions of 75-100K for several years you'd convert a big chunk but at a higher tax rate. At that point after 4-5 years you wouldn't have exhausted it completely but it would have a significantly smaller balance. At that point you could let it grow and keep doing conversions but at lower amounts of 25-30K and thus at a much lower tax rate.
No, it shouldn't. Your goal should be to maximize your after-tax dollars to spend (potentially covering your heirs as well) - whether that is best done by having zero Traditional IRAs or not doing any conversions at all is highly case specific.

I came of age during the Great Recession, when the Federal Reserve slashed interest rates to zero and kept them there for almost a decade. (The Fed cautiously started to raise rates a tiny bit in the late 2010s, only to slash them back to zero during the pandemic[1]FRED. Overnight Bank Funding Rate (OBFR). Accessed Oct 15, 2026. View all sources .)

So for most of my adult life, Treasury bonds paid basically nothing in yield. If you were looking to earn passive income as an investor, dividend stocks were pretty much the only game in town. If you’re under the age of ~40, this is probably true for you, too.

But we’re in a different world now. Benchmark rates (and bond yields) have generally gone up over the last five years, and if recent economic data is any indication, they could go even higher in the months ahead. (You can get caught up on the latest inflation reading in our write-up here[2]Bureau of Labor Statistics. Consumer Price Index Summary. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources .)

As I write this, the 3-month T-bill yield is around 4.07% and the 5-year note is getting close to 5%. You can see the yields for other Treasurys and savings rates in the table below:

That’s a lot higher than we’re used to seeing bond yields. It’s also a lot higher than quite a few dividend yields. In fact, it’s higher than the vast majority of yields in the Dividend Aristocrats index (a group of S&P 500 companies that have raised their dividend payouts annually for at least 25 years).

So if you’re looking for a dividend yield that’s higher than current bond yields, you’re probably looking at a risky dividend that could be cut. This raises an interesting question: Is dividend investing worth it in this age of high bond yields?

There isn’t a simple answer. Both dividend stocks and bonds have some unique advantages over each other. We’re breaking it down below.

Potentially higher yields. Treasury bonds now pay higher yields than the vast majority of the Dividend Aristocrats, but not all of them.

As noted on our page here that shows the top seven Dividend Aristocrats by yield, you can see yields range from 4.5% to 5.92% as of Oct. 16.

If you look at the broader universe of dividend stocks and dividend ETFs, there are even higher yields available.

More capital gains. Income isn’t everything. Both bonds and dividend stocks are also assets that have market prices. When it comes to price gains, dividend stocks still have a big advantage over bonds (in part because rising bond prices mean falling bond yields[3]Investor.gov. Investor Bulletin: Fixed Income Investments — When Interest Rates Go Up, Prices of Fixed-Rate Bonds Fall. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources ).

If you look at a chart of the ProShares S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats ETF (NOBL) compared to the iShares U.S. Treasury Bond ETF (GOVT), this becomes clear:

More frequent payments (sometimes). Treasury bonds and notes pay interest semiannually, while short-term bills are sold at a discount to their face value, meaning that you realize their yield when you cash them in at maturity for the face value[4]Treasury Direct. Understanding Pricing and Interest Rates. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources . That means that if you’re investing in individual Treasury securities, you’re going to wait at least three months (the shortest commonly marketed Treasury duration) between payments.

Many large-cap dividend stocks also pay out dividends quarterly, semiannually or annually, but there are some monthly dividend stocks. (We have a page that tracks the highest-yielding monthly dividend stocks.)

One caveat here: If you’re more of an ETF investor, you should note that there are ETFs that pay out monthly dividends that contain both dividend stocks and bonds. In fact, our page on the highest-yielding monthly dividend ETFs shows a mix of both.

» If these things appeal to you, check out our roundup of the best brokers for dividend investing.

Virtually no default risk. Treasurys are widely regarded as the benchmark for a risk-free investment worldwide. The risk of a default isn’t exactly zero (that’s technically not true of any investment), but Treasurys are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government, which oversees the largest national economy in the world.

A U.S. Treasury default is extremely unlikely, and it’s sort of a “giant asteroid” scenario — if it were to happen, it would precipitate an unprecedented global financial and political crisis, and “darn, I should have bought dividend stocks instead” would probably be the least of your worries.

State & local tax exemption. Income from Treasurys is taxable at the federal level, but not at the state and local levels[5]Investor.gov. Treasury Securities. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources , while dividend income is taxable at all three levels. That means that if you live in a high-tax jurisdiction, like I do (New York City greatest city in da world baybee), the after-tax yields of Treasurys compare even more favorably to those of dividend stocks.

Predictability. If you buy Treasurys and hold them to maturity, you are guaranteed by the U.S. government to earn the yield at the time of purchase. That dependability can make planning a lot easier, especially if you’re using short-term or mid-term Treasurys as more of a savings vehicle than an investment.

By contrast, dividend stocks are much less predictable. Stocks are more volatile than Treasurys. That gives them the potential for greater capital gains, as shown above, but it also gives them the potential for greater losses when the market gets turbulent.

Plus, dividend cuts do happen; they’re a much more substantial risk than the doomsday scenario of a Treasury default. Even Dividend Aristocrats, which are generally the most reliable dividend stocks, occasionally stop being Dividend Aristocrats and cut their dividends, as Walgreens Boots Alliance (WBA) did last year[6]Associated Press. #55. What Are Mutual Funds?

Some products in this article are from our partners. Read our Advertiser Discloser.

If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

Each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

When you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it plans to do it.

Investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund company or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

These funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

These funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most important things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

The problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

For most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

The expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

These are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

When you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

For investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

Most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly

This is the biggest issue with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

When a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an issue in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

It is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

With thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

That said, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most important step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

Deacon has been featured in many news publications including Yahoo Finance, US News & World Report, CNN Money, and more.

#59. Mezzi Review: The Proactive AI Financial Advisor For A Flat Fee

I have more than 40 financial accounts across four people to manage.

More accounts means more questions. Can we spend more? Are we missing a tax opportunity? Does an investment still make sense given everything else we own? For years, answering them meant a spreadsheet, a free Saturday, and a lot of analysis that leads to posts.

Then I started using Mezzi, an AI financial advisor. What hooked me is that it's an intelligent conversation. I can ask about my actual portfolio at 11 p.m., push back, and keep going until the answer makes sense. No awkward email. No dumb questions.

Better yet, Mezzi doesn't wait for me to ask. It flags losses worth harvesting, cheaper funds, positions that have grown too big, and lots that just turned long-term. I can also give it standing assignments, like reviewing my taxable accounts every week.

Within weeks, it showed my Google exposure was about $1.3 million, not the $900,000 to $1 million I'd guessed. My Nike loss was closer to $20,000, not $10,000, so I harvested it to offset gains elsewhere.

I like Mezzi so much that I invested in the company directly and am an affiliate partner. It is the most powerful AI investment advisor I've come across.

Mezzi advises on when you can retire, how to lower your taxes, and what to buy, hold, or sell. It charges a flat fee instead of a percentage of your assets, and your money stays where it is.

My first post covered the hidden stock exposure Mezzi found. This Mezzi review goes much further. We'll follow a hypothetical Bay Area couple to see how its advice works in real life, and whether it's worth paying for. It is.

Providing financial advice with AI is new. That’s one of the reasons I was excited to invest. And I invested before the release of a study by NYU Stern researcher Valerie Baldinger examining Mezzi’s recommendations and members’ investment decisions.

In a five-year historical comparison, portfolios built from Mezzi’s recommendations showed roughly 15% stronger risk-adjusted results than portfolios built from the same investors’ other purchases.

The study also found that investors shifted more new money toward broad index funds after starting to use Mezzi and selected lower-cost funds when they followed its recommendations, with annual expense ratios about 0.09 percentage points lower.

Mezzi is for people who want help working through life’s nuance to make better financial decisions and use their wealth to achieve their goals.

Mezzi’s average customer is a millionaire. Customers typically have meaningful assets spread across multiple accounts, and more financial complexity than they want to manage alone.

Whichever group you fall into, the questions often start the same way: Can I retire when I want? Am I missing tax opportunities? What should I do with my investments? The answers are intertwined, so this review follows one household through retirement, taxes, and investments.

Mezzi helps you work through that nuance in a natural conversation, much like talking with a human advisor, and get answers in seconds.

On Advisory and Concierge, there is no limit on how many questions you can ask. With a traditional advisor, you might hesitate to fire off another email or ask what feels like a dumb question. With Mezzi, you can ask as often as you like, at any hour, and keep following up until the answer makes sense. That advice starts with context.

For this review, we’ll follow a hypothetical family to see how Mezzi tailors its advice to their circumstances. Meet Manny and Melissa. Their situation is the context Mezzi works from.

Manny and Melissa are 45 and 40, respectively, with two children (5 and 10). They file taxes as married filing jointly, send their children to private school, and live in the San Francisco Bay Area. They want to pay for their children’s college education and expect a $500,000 inheritance from their parents. Their financial picture includes a smorgasbord of accounts:

Both of them want to retire around 55 and travel the world. One works a high-paying but volatile tech job, while the other has a stable career as a nurse.

They work with a traditional financial advisor for one brokerage account.

Mezzi captures your accounts, income sources, spending, tax details, family circumstances, goals, and more. Think of it as building the brain of your financial advisor.

Don’t worry, its brain won’t explode. And you decide what goes into it. So give it as much information as possible about your financial life.

The softer personal details matter just as much. Is the college money off-limits for retirement? Would you sell the family home? Are you willing to work part-time, or do you want to stop completely? Two families with the same net worth can need very different advice.

Mezzi brings together connected account data and the context you add through AI personalization. You can review and save it for future analysis, then update it through chat as life changes. With that fuller picture, a question like “Can I retire early?” becomes a much more useful conversation.

Saved personalization gives Mezzi context about your goals and everything that matters to you.

Mezzi’s Financial Profile helps Mezzi evaluate what you can spend, save, and invest.

Let’s say you want to retire early. Working another two years may make a retirement projection look better. Whether those two years are worth it is a more personal question. Perhaps you would rather work part-time, keep a rental property, or spend more time with your children. To weigh those choices, you need to see how your whole financial life supports them.

Mezzi can compare retirement dates, model Roth conversions, and work through which accounts to draw from first. Spending from connected accounts and the expenses you add help show what your retirement income needs to cover.

With that context saved, let’s ask whether Manny and Melissa can retire as planned, and what they might need to change.

What I like here is how Mezzi connects the retirement goal to useful decisions today. It shows Manny and Melissa where they stand, then recommends ways to strengthen their plan, including building cash reserves and reducing concentrated stock exposure.

Linked questions open in Mezzi using your own accounts and saved profile. An active account and any required setup are needed.

Figuring out whether you can retire early also means deciding how to adjust investments across your accounts to support that goal. Mezzi helps compare the tax consequences of rebalancing, identify losses to harvest, and examine dividend income and withdrawal order.

Here, Manny and Melissa ask which accounts to use to fund their retirement:

Mezzi considers continuing income and account tax treatment when recommending how to fund retirement.

Next, the conversation turns to what Melissa could hold in her solo 401(k), connecting fund selection to the same retirement goal.

The solo 401(k) recommendation pairs an allocation review with four specific portfolio adjustments.

What I love is that these recommendations consider portfolio risk alongside taxes. More on that in the investment section.

Of course, Mezzi can help with smaller decisions too. My first experience with its tax-aware guidance involved my Nike position. I thought my loss was about $10,000. Mezzi showed it was closer to $20,000, and I sold enough shares at a loss to offset long-term gains from other sales. I'm glad I did because Nike continued to decline by over 15% after my sale.

The same review is useful before a trade you are considering or one your advisor proposes. But I don’t want every opportunity to depend on remembering to ask.

Mezzi’s Delegations let you turn a tax question into ongoing work. Give Mezzi an assignment through chat, specifying what to review and when. Think of it as creating your own financial agent for a particular job. Instead of revisiting the same question each week, you can ask Mezzi to keep doing the analysis.

To me, Delegations are the most powerful way to use Mezzi, and a peek at where wealth management is heading. Instead of remembering to check every account, you hand Mezzi the monitoring and hear back when something needs a decision. That takes much of the ongoing work of managing your wealth off your plate.

In the separate example below, a Delegation email flags 10 positions with unrealized losses of $1,000 or more, led by Zoom Communications (-$9,907), Unity Software (-$7,092), and Crown Castle (-$6,838). Mezzi can repeat the review and notify you by email or on your iPhone. Check the schedule it confirms; you can change or remove the Delegation through chat.

Some monitoring happens without a Delegation at all. Mezzi’s Home screen surfaces insights on its own, each with a next step.

For Manny and Melissa, recent cards included a reminder that there is still time to fund their IRAs and 401(k)s this year, a Roth IRA that hit a new high with an option to see what drove it, and an estimate that switching to lower-cost funds could save about $2,255 in fees over five years.

Beyond recurring reviews and alerts, you can upload documents, such as a PDF or a screenshot, and Mezzi will analyze them alongside your accounts.

Take an employer 401(k) fund menu. Mezzi suggests an allocation from the plan’s options that fits your retirement timeline and what you already own elsewhere, with each fund’s fees shown beside it. In one example, it recommended a four-fund mix with expense ratios of 0.01% to 0.05%, while other funds on the same menu charged 0.65% to 0.80%.

Your tax return works the same way. For example:

Beyond taxes, I want to know what to own and how much. Mezzi provides investment recommendations, from reducing concentrated positions to choosing ETFs and finding lower-cost funds.

My Google experience brought that into focus. I had estimated my exposure at $900,000–$1 million. Once Mezzi included the Google shares held inside my funds, it was closer to $1.3 million. I was carrying more of the position than I realized.

Owning several funds can make a portfolio look diversified even when the same companies appear repeatedly. That is easy to miss when the funds sit at different institutions or some accounts are managed by an advisor while others are self-directed.

Mezzi’s Diversification X-ray combines the underlying holdings of supported funds with stocks owned directly, showing company and sector exposure across accounts.

Mezzi suggested trimming about $400,000. I chose to sell $200,000 in tax-advantaged accounts to avoid capital gains tax. I valued the analysis without following the recommendation in full. That is the kind of control I want to retain.

Back to Manny and Melissa, one of whom works in tech: here is how Mezzi weighs a Google sale across taxable and retirement accounts.

For a fuller look beyond these screenshots, watch this comprehensive Mezzi 101 with CEO Manish Jain.

Mezzi ships meaningful improvements every month, building on recent additions to wealth tracking, tax-lot detail, and Delegations.

Its broader ambition is an AI-native wealth management firm spanning advice, research, and eventually asset management. Asset management remains a roadmap ambition; Mezzi does not currently execute transactions.

Mezzi offers Free, Advisory, and Concierge memberships. The right plan depends on how much help you want.

Free: Start here if you mainly want the full picture. You can connect all your assets and liabilities, add a family member, and run the Diversification X-ray, but AI insights are limited. Great if you don’t want advice.

Advisory ($39 a month or $399 a year): It adds unlimited tax, retirement, and investment advice, five active Delegations, and support by video, phone, and email. Five Delegations cover a typical setup, such as a weekly tax-loss review, a monthly retirement check, and a daily news digest on your largest holdings.

Concierge ($99 a month or $999 a year): It unlocks unlimited Delegations so you can have Mezzi monitor anything 24/7. You’ll also get access to advanced AI models for more complex analysis, and quarterly platform coaching. The coaching is great if you are newer to AI and want one-on-one assistance with getting the most out of Mezzi. Coaching doesn’t mean financial advice—all financial advice is delivered by AI.

For comparison, some financial planners charge $400 an hour, and planning engagements can run $2,500–$10,000 depending on scope and complexity.

At a 1% annual advisory fee, a constant $1 million portfolio costs $10,000 a year, compared with $399 for annual Mezzi Advisory. The services are not identical: a human advisor may also handle implementation and provide personal support. Fund expenses and other investment costs remain separate.

If you want to hand your money to someone and never think about it again, Mezzi isn't for you. It doesn't (yet) execute trades, assign you a dedicated human advisor, prepare your tax returns, or draft your estate documents. You still pull the trigger, and you may still need a CPA or estate attorney.

Personally, I see that as a feature. After 13 years in finance, as a DIY investor, I don't want anyone moving my money without my say. Mezzi does the analysis and the monitoring. I keep the final call. That's how I sold $200,000 of Google instead of the $400,000 it suggested, without arguing with anybody.

Mezzi also isn't for someone with a three-fund portfolio and a process they already follow without fail. If that's you, congratulations. You probably don't need another subscription. It's built for U.S. households, and like any advisor, human or AI, its advice is only as good as the information you give it.

But if you've got multiple accounts, a few moving parts, and more decisions than free Saturdays, Mezzi earns its keep, and then some.

If that sounds like you, the next questions are practical: how your accounts connect, who can see your information, and how Mezzi fits with the services you already use. Let's go through them.

Mezzi is a financial advisor, not just a personal finance dashboard. Tracking accounts, spending, and projections helps you understand your finances. Mezzi uses that information to recommend what to do: how much to save, which investments to buy or sell, and how to coordinate tax and retirement decisions.

You can question a recommendation, compare alternatives, and assign ongoing reviews. The value is personalized advice and follow-through, not simply another place to see your accounts.

It was harder than anyone expected. The product never quite worked as planned, and the team ended up being acquired by a larger financial institution a year after I left.

So I appreciate how easy Mezzi makes it. Now both of you can ask questions, see the same recommendations, and stop having the “wait, how much is in that account?” conversation at dinner.

Every investor I know thinks they're above average. I used to think so too. Then I started asking Mezzi hard questions about my own portfolio, and my ego took a few body blows.

That's why I'll keep using Mezzi as my interactive guide. Its job is to keep me honest about my performance and my risk, because my ego certainly won't. The bigger and messier your portfolio gets, the easier it is to fool yourself. Having an AI advisor that never sleeps, never gets annoyed by follow-up questions, and never tells you what you want to hear is worth a lot.

Give Mezzi a try and see what blind spots or opportunities it finds in your portfolio. Worst case, you confirm you're as savvy as you think. Best case, you catch something before it costs you.

#60. Debt And Physician Finances
