#167. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Yay! I’m thrilled to read about a city of the future, and I look forward to hearing more when you spend the winter there. I gave them my email address so I could hear more in the future.

Mostly because of distances, I’d say. The US are huge compared to Europe (and still mostly empty – to the point that cities spread horizontally to infinity rather than vertically – except San Francisco and Manhattan that are peninsulas).

In Europe, streets have always been very narrow because initially built just for humans and horses. This makes Europe perfect for biking + walking only. The countries and cities are much smaller, too. And since the population density is also way higher in Europe, they have all incentives to keep it human-friendly.

Also, the US are the 3rd oil producer in the world. Europe, with the exception for Norway, has little to no oil. In other words, the US were incentivized to push for oil consumption (good for the economy – with a 1900s mindset obviously). Europe, not so much, since oil is imported and as a result more expensive.

If you fly one airline with a partner or child at least once a year, a companion certificate from an airline credit card can save you more than the card’s annual fee. Before you count on it, check which fares and routes it covers, what taxes you still pay, and when it expires.

The certificate puts a second traveler on your round trip for the taxes and fees alone, or on some cards for a small set fare plus taxes.

The $350-a-year Delta SkyMiles Platinum American Express Card gives you one after each renewal, good for a Delta Main (economy) round trip within the U.S. or to destinations Delta lists in Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America. On a round trip of up to four flights, the companion pays at most $80 in taxes and fees within the U.S. and $250 abroad. The $650-a-year Delta SkyMiles Reserve‘s certificate also covers the roomier Delta Comfort and Delta First cabins.

On the $95-a-year Atmos Rewards Ascent Visa Signature for Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines flyers, the companion pays $99 plus taxes and fees that start at $23. That fare arrives each card anniversary only if you charged $6,000 or more in purchases the year before.

Four rules in Delta’s terms decide what its certificate is worth to you:

Then price a trip you’d take anyway. Say you and a partner fly Delta Main nonstop within the U.S. each year, and an eligible fare costs $450 a seat, round trip with taxes. With the certificate, the second seat costs $80 or less, so you save at least $370, $20 more than the Platinum’s $350 fee.

This math works on any card. Before each renewal, check whether the second seat on your travel dates would cost more than the fee plus what the companion still owes, $430 on the trip above.

#179. Pre-Authorization Holds Aren’t Charges – Get the Merchant’s Release, Then Call Your Bank

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A pre-authorization hold sets aside part of your available credit or checking balance until the merchant’s final charge replaces it. If a hold is blocking money or credit you need, ask the merchant to release it and send you written confirmation, then share that confirmation with your bank so it can lift the hold early.

A $150 pending charge from the gas station after a $48 fill-up looks like an overcharge. It’s a hold the station placed before you started pumping, and it drops to $48 once the station sends the final amount.

Merchants place a hold when they don’t know the final total at the moment you pay. A hotel holds the nightly rate plus extra for charges like room service, a car rental counter holds a deposit, and a restaurant may hold extra in case you add a tip. A hold shows in your account as pending rather than posted, and no money reaches the merchant until the final charge goes through. A pending charge you can’t match to anywhere you used your card may be fraud, so report it to your card issuer right away.

That final charge normally replaces the hold. If your bank can’t match the two, which can happen when the amounts differ, the hold stays until it expires, and one purchase can look like two for a few days. Most holds fall off within a week, though hotel and car rental holds can last until you check out or return the car, plus a few days.

The merchant decides how much to hold, and your bank decides how long it lasts. Some banks lift a hold early only once the merchant has released it, so when one is blocking money or credit you need, take these steps in order.

If a hold still hasn’t changed after a week, ask the merchant whether the sale was completed or canceled, then ask your bank when the hold is set to expire.

Before you apply for a credit card, check for six common triggers of a denial: a low score, high card balances, recent applications, a thin credit history, low income, and a credit freeze. Start at least a month ahead, so you can pay balances down and lift any freeze before an issuer pulls your report.

A denied application still costs you. The issuer’s credit check, called a hard inquiry, stays on your credit report for two years, where other issuers can see it.

Issuers decide mostly from your credit reports, your score, and the income you list, so you can spot each trigger before they do.

Pull your free credit reports from all three bureaus at AnnualCreditReport.com, then run these checks at least a month before you apply:

Say you owe $3,500 on cards with $5,000 in combined limits, a 70% utilization rate. Pay $2,500 before your statements close, when issuers typically report balances, and your reports will show 20%, not 70%, by the time you apply.

Then apply for one card, and wait at least six months before the next, since each application adds a hard inquiry.

If a check turns up a thin file or several recent applications, which take months to change, set a date to check again instead of applying.

#187. How a Credit Card Works – You Pay the Statement, Not Each Purchase

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A credit card lets you borrow up to a set limit, and each monthly statement shows what you owe, a minimum payment, and a due date at least 21 days later. Find all four numbers in your card’s app. Most cards charge interest on purchases only when part of a statement balance goes unpaid past its due date.

Your card doesn’t bill you for each purchase. It runs on monthly billing cycles, and whatever you owe on the last day of a cycle, called the closing date, becomes your statement balance.

Your due date falls at least 21 days after the statement closes, on the same day every month. Most cards also have a grace period, meaning purchases cost no interest when you pay the full statement balance by the due date. Say yours does and you start a cycle owing nothing. Your only purchase that cycle, $400 on June 3, goes on the statement that closes June 25, which is due July 20. Pay the $400 by July 20 and you owe no interest.

Spend $60 more on June 28 and your current balance, the running total in the app, becomes $460. Your statement balance stays $400, and the $60 goes on the July statement, due August 20.

In your card’s app, the account details show your minimum payment, your due date, and your credit limit, the most you can owe at once. The statement balance is on each statement the app saves. The minimum is the smallest amount due that month, and paying only that means interest on the rest of the balance.

Know three costs up front. The APR, or annual percentage rate, is the yearly interest rate the card charges. Missing the minimum payment by the due date can add a late fee, and your statement lists its amount beside that date. A cash advance, cash you withdraw with the card, usually charges interest from day one, at a higher rate than purchases, plus a fee.

Find your closing date and due date in the app today, and set a monthly reminder a few days before the due date.

Your 0% balance transfer offer can pay off a car or personal loan if its terms cover balance transfer checks, a deposit to your checking account, or a payment straight to your lender. Move the loan when the fee costs less than the interest you’d otherwise pay and you can clear the new balance before the 0% ends.

A car or personal loan charges interest every month. A 0% transfer charges a one-time fee, usually 3% to 5% of what you move, and no interest until the promotion ends, typically 12 to 21 months later.

Say you owe the last $6,000 on a 9% car loan and pay $400 a month. Like most car loans, it charges interest on the remaining balance. Your offer is 18 months at 0% for a 3% fee. Keep paying the loan, and it charges about $390 in interest before it’s paid off in 16 months. Move it, and the $180 fee is added to the card balance, so $400 a month clears $6,180 in 16 months, two months before the 0% ends. You pay $180 instead of about $390, roughly $210 less.

First, confirm the offer covers a loan. Its 0% rate has to apply to balance transfer checks you write to the lender, a deposit into your checking account, or a payment the issuer sends the lender directly. Issuers also won’t pay off a loan from their own bank.

Next, get the lender’s payoff amount, which includes interest through the day the money arrives. Add the fee, divide by the months left at 0%, and set autopay for at least that amount, $344 in the example. Keep paying the loan until it shows as paid off, since a transfer can take three weeks.

The move raises your credit utilization, the share of your card limits in use, which can lower your score. A payment more than 60 days late lets the issuer end the 0% rate, and any balance left when the promotion ends starts accruing interest at the card’s regular rate, often above 20%. Keep new purchases off the card, too, as with any balance transfer.

A higher fee can wipe out the savings. With a 5% fee, the same move saves only about $90, and on a 6% loan, the $300 fee costs more than the roughly $250 in interest it would replace. If the fee is the bigger number, keep paying the lender.

#193. Credit Card Chargebacks Are Decided on Evidence – Gather Yours Before You Dispute

A credit card chargeback reverses a disputed charge, but the temporary credit your card issuer usually posts isn’t final. The merchant can answer with its own evidence, and the rules of your card’s network, such as Visa or Mastercard, decide who wins. Before you file, gather the receipt, the merchant’s policy, your messages, and photos of the problem.

Your $640 espresso machine arrives with a cracked water tank, and the merchant refuses a refund because you opened the box. You dispute the charge, and your issuer takes the $640 off your balance while it investigates.

The issuer sends the dispute through the card network to the merchant’s bank, and the merchant gets a deadline to respond. For a damaged item, Visa’s guide for merchants tells them to send an invoice showing the item was as described, or to say you never tried to return it. If the issuer finds the merchant’s case stronger than yours, the credit comes off and the $640 goes back on your bill.

The same guide tells merchants their return policy doesn’t matter in a dispute over damaged goods. So on a Visa card, the merchant can’t win your dispute just by citing its rule about opened boxes. Policies do matter when you canceled an order or service, since the merchant can argue you didn’t follow its cancellation terms.

Expect a decision in a few weeks to about three months.

Never dispute a purchase you made and only regret. The merchant’s proof that you placed the order will likely cost you the credit, and an issuer that sees you do it repeatedly can close your account.

Read your documents the way the issuer will, without your explanation to fill the gaps. If they show what you were promised, what you got, and that you tried to fix it, send them.

If you’re 18 with income or assets of your own, start building credit with one student, starter, or secured card. Put a single small recurring bill on it and set autopay to pay the full statement balance every month. That builds the on-time payments and low balances that count most in your credit score.

At 18 you likely have no credit history, and FICO can’t score you until an account is at least six months old. The clock starts when your first one opens.

That account doesn’t need to do much. Payment history makes up 35% of a typical FICO score and how much you owe another 30%. Your card issuer sends both to the credit bureaus every month, generally on the day your statement closes. One small charge paid in full puts an on-time payment and a low balance on your record each month, interest-free.

Student cards need no deposit, and some starter cards are made for people new to credit. A secured card takes a refundable deposit that typically becomes your limit. You can also be added to a parent’s card as an authorized user, or take out a credit-builder loan, which holds the money in savings until you’ve repaid it.

Until you turn 21, federal rules require income or assets of your own that cover a card’s minimum payments, or a co-signer who is at least 21. Pay from a part-time job counts. A parent’s income doesn’t, and secured cards follow the same rule.

Six months in, you’ll have a FICO score backed by on-time payments. Keep that first card open after you move on to better ones, since the length of your credit history makes up 15% of a typical FICO score.

Before you close an unused credit card, check what it costs you. A card with no annual fee costs nothing to keep and still helps your credit, so leave it open. Downgrade or close only the cards that charge a fee you don’t earn back or tempt you to overspend.

How much you use a card is the wrong test for closing it. The card you never touch is often the no-fee card you opened first.

That card is worth keeping open. Its limit adds to your total credit limit, which keeps down your credit utilization, the share of that total you’re using. And as it ages, it keeps lengthening your credit history.

A card with an annual fee charges you every year, used or not, so a $95 card you’ve stopped using costs $95 a year for nothing. A card that tempts you into extra spending costs money too, even with no fee. Those costs, not how rarely you use a card, are the reason to close one.

Sort each card by its annual fee, its age, its limit, and whether it tempts you. Then make one of three moves.

If a card still has to go, close the newest one with the smallest limit. That removes the least from your total limit and leaves your oldest accounts open. Redeem its rewards first, since you can lose them when the account closes.

Say you have five cards. You’d keep the three oldest no-fee cards on small recurring charges and switch the $95 travel card you stopped using to a no-fee card. The store card you opened last year still tempts you after you put it away, and it has your smallest limit, so you’d redeem its rewards and close it.

Pull out every card this week and sort it before you cancel any of them.

#202. Chase’s 5/24 Rule Applies to Ink Business Cards – Count Your Personal Cards First

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. If you’ve opened at least five personal credit cards with any bank over the last two years, Chase will likely deny your Ink business card application under its unofficial 5/24 rule. Count yours first, closed and authorized-user cards included, and get the Chase cards you want before opening personal cards elsewhere.

Chase doesn’t publish the rule, but applicants’ reported approvals and denials show that it counts cards from your personal credit report. That means the personal cards you’ve opened decide whether you get a business one.

Chase counts every credit card your report shows as opened in the past 24 months, from any bank, even one you’ve since closed. That includes cards someone else added you to as an authorized user, because they appear on your report even though you aren’t responsible for the bill. Most business cards don’t count, since they don’t appear on personal reports, and that includes the Ink card you’re applying for. The exceptions are business cards from Discover and TD Bank, plus most of Capital One’s, which do appear and count.

To check where you stand, pull your free reports from all three credit bureaus at AnnualCreditReport.com and list each card’s open date. Plan on a card counting until the first of the month after it turns two, so one opened March 10 stops counting on April 1 two years later. If an authorized-user card is what puts you at five, Chase’s reconsideration line, which reviews denied applications, may agree to leave it out of the count.

Your count also decides which card to apply for first. Say you’ve opened four personal cards in the past 24 months, so you’re at 4/24, and you want an Ink card plus a personal card from another bank. Apply for the Ink first, and you’re still at 4/24 afterward. Open the other card first, and you’re at 5/24, so Chase will likely decline the Ink until your oldest card stops counting.

When you do apply, the Ink application asks for your business’s legal structure, start date, and annual revenue, and the card makes you personally liable for the balance along with your business.

Check your count before every card application while a Chase card is still on your list, since a fifth personal card from any bank can put Chase off-limits for months.

Of all the numbers on your credit card, the three- or four-digit security code is the one to guard, because stores aren’t allowed to keep it after a sale. Enter it only at a checkout you started yourself, and never send it by email or text.

That matters because online, you type the printed numbers instead of handing over the card, and so can anyone who steals them. The chip and the contactless symbol, four curved lines, only come into play when you pay in person.

Start with the long card number. Its first digit names the payment network, with 4 for Visa, 5 or 2 for Mastercard, 3 for American Express, and 6 for Discover. That network’s logo on the card shows where you can use it. The first six to eight digits identify the bank that issued the card, the digits after that identify your account, and the last digit lets a checkout form catch a mistyped number. The expiration date is the last month the card works, through that month’s final day.

The security code, often called the CVV, is three digits on the back of most cards and four on the front of an American Express card. Online stores ask for it to help confirm you’re holding the card, and the card industry’s security rules bar them from saving it once a purchase is approved. So a card number stolen from a store’s records shouldn’t come with the code, and a thief without the code can’t finish a purchase at a checkout that requires it.

These habits keep the code, and the rest of your card details, away from thieves:

If you think someone else has your code, call your card issuer right away for a replacement card, which comes with a new code.

If you carry a credit card balance most months, new purchases collect interest from the day you make them, and that interest soon costs more than any rewards they earn. Switch everyday spending to debit until the balance is gone, then go back to credit once you can pay in full every month.

It’s time to switch if interest shows up on most statements, you pay the minimum or close to it, or your spending rose when your credit limit did.

Say your card charges a 22% APR, its yearly interest rate, and pays 2% cash back. Carrying a balance cancels the grace period, the interest-free stretch before your due date, so a $100 grocery run starts collecting interest the day you buy it. That interest runs about $1.83 a month. Two months in, the purchase has cost about $3.70 in interest and earned $2 back, so you’re $1.70 behind.

Switching to debit stops the balance from growing. With your daily spending off the card, every payment shrinks the balance, and the money in checking limits what you can spend.

To step back without hurting your credit:

Debit has risks of its own. Tell your bank to turn off overdraft coverage for debit purchases. Then a purchase your balance can’t cover is declined instead of going through with a fee.

Keep a cushion in checking, too. Gas pumps, hotels, and rental car counters can put a hold on more money than you spend, and the hold can last for days. Debit’s fraud protection is also weaker than a credit card’s, so report any strange charge right away.

When the balance hits zero, switch autopay to the full statement balance. After you’ve paid three statements in full, bring everyday spending back to the card.

Pay a store card’s balance in full by the first due date, and its checkout discount is yours to keep. If you’d carry the purchase instead, a year of interest at the card’s rate, often above 30%, can cost as much as the discount saves. That’s still cheaper than carrying it on a typical credit card.

Say the clerk offers 15% off a $600 TV if you open the store’s card today. That’s $90 off. But pay off the remaining $510 in 12 equal monthly payments at a 30% annual percentage rate (APR), and by our math the interest comes to about $87.

That leaves you about $3 ahead of paying $600 up front. If you’d carry the TV either way, the store card is still cheaper than a general-purpose card, at the cost of a hard inquiry on your credit report. Those averaged a 25% APR in 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) found. By our math, 12 payments on $600 at that rate cost about $84 in interest, so the store card comes out about $88 ahead. Store-only cards averaged 31%, and many charge every cardholder the same rate, so strong credit won’t get you a lower one.

FICO says a hard inquiry takes less than five points off most people’s scores and stops counting after a year. If your credit is strong, a store-only card’s starting limit is typically less than half what a general-purpose card would give you, the CFPB found. So the same $510 balance takes up a bigger share of the limit. That raises your credit utilization, which can lower your score until you pay it down.

After the first purchase, the card is worth using only if you shop there constantly and pay it in full every month. If you shop there only now and then, a no-annual-fee card that earns 2% back on everything you buy is the better everyday card. For the store’s rewards, ask whether it also offers a co-branded card, which many big retailers do. It carries the store’s name but works at other stores too.

Financing that’s interest-free only if you pay in full by a deadline is deferred interest, a different deal with risks of its own.

Take the discount only on something you came to buy, and pay the card off before you charge anything else to it.

If you carry a credit card balance, call your card issuer and ask it to cut your interest rate. Issuers grant most of these requests, and each percentage point off saves about $10 a year for every $1,000 you owe. Lead with your on-time payment record and a better offer from another card.

In LendingTree’s 2026 survey, only 23% of cardholders had asked for a lower APR, the yearly interest rate on a card balance, in the previous 12 months.

Of those who did, 84% got a lower rate, and the average cut was 6.3 percentage points. On a $6,000 balance, a six-point cut from 28% to 22% saves about $360 a year in interest for as long as you carry it.

Before you call, have four things in front of you.

Call the customer service number on your card and keep the pitch short. “I’ve paid this card on time for six years, and my rate is 28%. I have an offer for a card at 20%, and I’d rather stay with you. Can you lower my rate?” Before the rep reviews your account, ask whether the review involves a hard credit check, which can happen when an issuer treats the request as an account change.

If the first rep can’t lower the rate, ask for a supervisor or the retention department, whose job is keeping customers. When the answer is yes, ask whether the new rate is permanent or promotional and, if it’s promotional, when it ends.

If it’s still no, try again in a few months or move the balance. A 0% balance transfer card stops interest on the moved balance for its promotional period. It usually takes good credit to get one, and the one-time fee is typically 3% to 5% of the amount moved. A debt consolidation loan can pay off the card instead. Compare its APR, which includes its fees, with your card’s. If you’re struggling to keep up, ask about the issuer’s hardship program, which can lower your rate temporarily. Then give your other monthly bills the same call.

Before you compare credit card rewards, decide whether you’ll ever carry a balance. If you might, weigh the interest a lower rate or a long 0% intro offer would save against the rewards you’d give up. If you always pay in full, ignore the rate and choose on rewards and fees.

Answer with what you’ve done, not what you intend. If you’ve carried a balance in the past year, or a surprise bill would land on the card, shop as someone who carries one.

In LendingTree’s June survey, new cash back cards averaged about 24% APR, the card’s yearly interest rate, and low-interest cards about 17%. By our math, the lower rate saves about $70 a year per $1,000 carried, as much as a 2% card earns on $3,500 of purchases.

Carrying a balance also ends the interest-free grace period, so interest starts on new purchases the day you make them.

If you might carry a balance, compare cards’ ongoing APRs, the rates left once any promotion ends. A 0% intro APR on purchases or balance transfers gives you interest-free months, so pick one long enough to pay off what you owe. A balance transfer usually costs 3% to 5% of the amount moved. Favor cards without a penalty APR, a rate that can jump to around 30% after a missed payment.

If you always pay in full, the APR drops out of the decision, since most cards charge no interest on purchases paid off by the due date. Match the rewards to where you spend, and pay an annual fee only when the extra rewards beat it.

Either way, run three checks before you apply. Target cards built for your credit score, since applying triggers a hard credit check that can lower your score, approved or not. Prequalify where the issuer offers it, because prequalifying uses a soft check that doesn’t affect your score. Then read the pricing table that card applications must include, which lists the annual, foreign transaction, and late fees beside the APRs.

Revisit the choice when your habits change. Twelve straight months with no balance is your cue to ignore the rate.

#226. The Five-Year Test – When Bankruptcy Beats Trying to Repay Your Debt

Filing for bankruptcy makes sense when your credit card and medical debt couldn’t be repaid within five years, even on a credit counseling plan. Multiply what you can spare each month by 60. If that falls far short of what you owe, stop cashing out your 401(k) to keep up and talk to a bankruptcy attorney.

Treat bankruptcy as a moral failure and you’ll keep paying long after the math stops working, even if that means emptying a 401(k) or borrowing against your house for debts bankruptcy would have erased.

Filing is a legal tool, not a verdict on your character.

Start with the five-year test. Add up your unsecured debt, the kind not tied to a house or car, like credit cards, medical bills, and personal loans. Subtract essentials like housing, food, utilities, and insurance from your monthly take-home pay, then multiply what’s left by 60, the months in a long credit counseling plan. If that total, which leaves out interest, falls far short of the debt, no repayment plan will close the gap.

Say you owe $60,000, $50,000 of it on credit cards, and can spare $300 a month. Sixty payments total $18,000, under a third of the balance. At typical card rates above 20%, the card interest alone tops $800 a month, nearly three times the payment.

Once the test points to bankruptcy, stop paying with money it protects. Bankruptcy shields 401(k)s fully and IRAs up to a seven-figure cap, so cashing one out spends savings you’d keep, and before age 59½ it usually adds a 10% penalty to the income tax. A home equity loan turns card debt bankruptcy could erase into debt secured by your house.

Don’t file over a balance the test says you can repay, or one made up mostly of debts bankruptcy won’t erase, like child support and recent taxes. If an inheritance or other lump sum is coming, rerun the test with it, since an inheritance you’re entitled to within 180 days after filing can go to creditors.

Recent large charges are a reason to wait a few months. Luxury purchases within 90 days of filing and cash advances within 70 days, above set dollar limits, are presumed to survive the bankruptcy.

Weigh the numbers against filing’s fees and seven to 10 years on your credit report, with a bankruptcy attorney or a nonprofit credit counselor, and decide while your retirement savings are still intact.

Check your credit card’s guide to benefits before you pay for a store’s extended warranty. Many cards add a year to the manufacturer’s warranty at no extra cost on items bought with the card, so the store’s plan can duplicate coverage you already have. Keep the receipt and warranty in case the item breaks.

The pitch usually comes at the register. You’ve picked out a refrigerator or a laptop, and the cashier asks whether you want to protect it for a few more years. Before you answer, know what your card already covers.

Chase’s Freedom and Sapphire cards add one year to eligible manufacturer’s warranties of three years or less. The American Express Gold Card adds up to a year to warranties of five years or less.

Charge a $900 refrigerator with a one-year warranty to one of those cards, and a breakdown the manufacturer would have fixed in year one is covered in year two. So pay for a plan only for what it covers beyond the card’s year.

Buying the plan can even cost you the card’s year. Chase’s coverage starts only after any plan you buy runs out and ends four years after the purchase, so a plan that runs through year four leaves the card nothing to add.

Before your next big purchase, find out which card in your wallet adds the extra year, and make it the one you hand the cashier.

Credit card payment protection charges a monthly fee on your balance for limited help after a layoff, disability, or death. Turn it down, and cancel it if it’s already on your statement. If your income drops, ask your issuer whether you qualify for a hardship program. It’s free, but it usually lowers your payment rather than making it for you.

Issuers that sell it often pitch it when you call to activate a card or reach customer service. Buying it is always optional, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau warns that add-ons sold this way can deliver less than buyers expect.

The fee is a set amount for every $100 of your statement balance, so it grows as you owe more. At 89 cents per $100, a $6,000 balance costs $53.40 a month, or $640.80 a year. The charge applies even if you pay your bill in full each month, because it’s figured on the balance your statement shows.

Coverage is narrower than the pitch. After a layoff or disability, plans typically make only your minimum payment, and only for a limited number of months. Credit One Bank’s plan, for one, covers up to six minimum payments while interest keeps building on the balance. If you die, it pays off no more than $10,000. Many plans won’t pay for a job loss in your first 30 days of coverage. Quitting, retiring, or getting fired for misconduct doesn’t qualify, and some plans require you to have worked at least 20 or 30 hours a week.

Look for a monthly charge on your statement named something like credit protection, payment protection, or payment security. If you find one, call the number on your card and cancel it. Plans let you cancel anytime, and some refund the fees if you do it soon after enrolling.

Then save the money instead. At $53.40 a month, you’d build an emergency fund of more than $640 within a year, and it can pay rent and groceries as well as a card bill.

If your income drops, call your issuer before your next due date and ask for a hardship program. It’s free, but the issuer decides who qualifies, and it usually lowers your rate or payment rather than paying the bill for you. If others depend on your paycheck, get quotes for term life or disability insurance.

If you pay for protection, buy the kind that pays you or your family, not your card issuer.

Bankruptcy wipes out most credit card, medical, and personal loan debt, but child support, alimony, recent income taxes, and most student loans survive it. Before you file, check which of your debts it would erase. If the ones you most need gone would survive, filing leaves your real problem in place.

Picture someone whose biggest debts are last year’s income taxes and back child support. Chapter 7 would wipe out their credit card balances and leave both standing.

Bankruptcy law sorts debts into three groups, and the discharge, the court order that releases you from debts, treats each one differently. General unsecured debts, like credit cards, medical bills, and personal loans, are the ones it usually erases.

Priority debts, which get repaid before general unsecured debts, include child support, alimony, and recent income taxes, all of which survive. Secured debts, like the loan on your house or car, stay tied to the property. The discharge ends what you personally owe, but the lender can still take the property if you stop paying.

The law also lists other debts that survive, including most student loans, criminal fines, and debts for injuries you caused while driving impaired. Debts from fraud survive only if the creditor challenges them in court and wins.

Older income taxes can be erased only if they pass three timing tests:

A fraudulent return or tax evasion keeps a tax from being erased, however old it is, and some federal appeals courts won’t erase tax on any return filed late.

To keep a financed car or house in Chapter 7, you can reaffirm the loan, signing an agreement to keep owing it after the discharge. Fall behind later, and the lender may be able to take your wages, not just the property. No law requires reaffirming, but a car lender may take back a car you neither reaffirm nor redeem by paying its current value at once.

Total up what would survive before you pay a lawyer or a filing fee. If it’s most of what you owe, a discharge won’t give you the fresh start you’re filing for.

Before you redeem credit card points, subtract any taxes you’d still pay from the cash price of what you’re getting, divide by the points it costs, and multiply by 100 for cents per point. If your points can go to cash back or travel at about a cent each, as Chase Ultimate Rewards points can, skip anything under that.

Points don’t come with a fixed price. The same 25,000 points can book a $500 flight, with $10 in taxes to pay, or buy a $200 gift card. That’s a $290 difference on one balance.

The math takes a minute. Take the cash price of the flight, gift card, or item, subtract any taxes or fees you’d still owe when paying with points, divide by the points required, and multiply by 100 to get cents per point.

The flight works out to $490 divided by 25,000, or 1.96 cents per point. The $200 gift card for the same 25,000 points comes to 0.8 cents.

Use a cent per point as your floor for bank points, such as Chase Ultimate Rewards, American Express Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou points, and Capital One miles. Each of those programs offers at least one easy redemption worth about a cent, either cash back or travel booked through the card’s own site. Anything below that pays you less than an option you already have. Hotel points run lower, about 0.4 cent for Hilton and 0.7 cent for Marriott in NerdWallet’s 2026 estimates, so measure a hotel redemption against its program’s typical value instead.

The convenient redemptions are where points lose value. Merchandise from a card’s rewards catalog can price points at half a cent. Gift cards run from half a cent to a cent, depending on the program and the store. Paying with points at a big online retailer’s checkout returns 0.7 or 0.8 cents a point with those bank programs.

Transfers to airline and hotel partners can push a point well past a cent. If cash is all you ever take, check whether a cash-back card would pay you more than your points do.

Do the division before every redemption. With bank points, if the option in front of you comes in under a cent, skip it and take the redemption that pays a cent.

#238. Credit Cards Beat Debit on Protection and Rewards – If You Pay in Full

A credit card beats a debit card on fraud protection, the right to dispute charges, rewards, and building credit. But carry a balance, and on average the interest and fees outweigh the rewards. Put everyday spending on credit only if you pay the full balance every month.

Debit feels safer because it spends money you already have. That’s also why fraud or a seller who never delivers hits your own cash, while a credit card puts the card issuer’s money at stake first.

If a thief runs up charges, federal law caps your loss at $50 on a credit card. On debit, that cap depends on how fast you report the theft, and the stolen money leaves checking first. If a purchase never arrives, the Fair Credit Billing Act lets you dispute the charge and hold back that amount while the issuer investigates. Debit purchases don’t get that right. Some cards also insure new purchases and rental cars. Rewards cards return 1% to 2% or more of what you spend, and on-time payments build a credit history. Most debit cards do neither.

Then come the costs. Carry a balance and you pay interest averaging more than 20% a year, according to Federal Reserve data. Interest on new purchases then starts the day you buy. Late fees, and on some cards an annual fee, add more. A credit limit, not your checking balance, caps your spending, which makes overspending easy. A payment 30 days late can stay on your credit reports for seven years, and balances near your limit can lower your scores.

So the deciding question is whether you pay the full balance every month. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau found that cardholders who carry a balance pay 94% of all credit card interest and fees but collect less than 30% of the rewards. On average, what they pay outweighs what they earn.

Check your last few statements. If none shows an interest charge, make credit your everyday card. If interest shows up month after month, lean on debit until the balance is paid off.

Before each charge, ask whether checking could cover it today. If it couldn’t, the purchase can wait.

#240. Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 Bankruptcy – Your Income and Property Usually Decide

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Two facts settle most of the choice between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 bankruptcy. Income above your state’s median for your household size means a second test for Chapter 7. Property a Chapter 7 trustee could sell, like home equity, points to Chapter 13, which lets you keep it. Check both before you call a lawyer.

Within a few months, Chapter 7 wipes out most debts with no collateral behind them, but a bankruptcy trustee can sell any property the law doesn’t protect. Chapter 13 lets you keep your property while you repay creditors through a three- to five-year plan.

The first fact is your income. The means test compares your average income over the six months before you file, at a yearly rate, with your state’s median for a household your size. Below it, Chapter 7 is open to you. Above it, a second step subtracts the expenses and loan payments the law allows and projects what’s left over five years. If that sum reaches the law’s threshold, the court can dismiss a Chapter 7 case, which leaves Chapter 13.

The second fact is what you own. Your state’s exemptions, or a federal list where the state allows it, decide what you keep. In most Chapter 7 cases filed by individuals, everything is exempt or tied to a loan, so the trustee sells nothing. Chapter 13 lets you keep equity beyond your exemptions, as long as your plan pays creditors at least what a Chapter 7 sale would have paid them.

Run both checks before your first consultation. Find your state’s figure in the U.S. Trustee Program’s means-testing tables and compare your income with it. Then list what you own, what each item is worth, what you owe on it, and any payment you’re behind on.

A renter with low income and few assets usually files Chapter 7. A homeowner with steady income who’s behind on the mortgage usually files Chapter 13, because its plan can catch up the missed payments over time and save the house. Chapter 13 also leaves your credit report sooner, since Experian keeps a Chapter 7 for 10 years from filing and a Chapter 13 for seven.

Take your numbers and your list to a free consultation with a bankruptcy lawyer, who can run the full means test and confirm the chapter before you file.

Missing your credit card’s minimum payment starts a clock. A late fee can hit right away, a credit report mark at 30 days, a penalty rate at 60, and collections near 180. Each stage is easier to stop than the one after it, so call your issuer before the due date and pay the missed minimum before day 30.

The first month is your window, because card issuers don’t report a late payment to the credit bureaus until it’s 30 days past due. A late fee can hit right after the due date, but federal rules cap it at your missed minimum payment.

Once the issuer reports the late payment, it can stay seven years on your credit report, counted from the date you first fell behind. At 60 days late, the issuer can apply any penalty rate your card carries to the balance you already owe, not just to new purchases. Around 180 days late, it writes off the account as a loss, called a charge-off, and may send or sell the debt to a collection agency. You still owe it, and the charge-off can stay on your report until seven years after the first missed payment.

Check your statement, which lists the late fee and any penalty rate a late payment can trigger. Then start with the earliest step you still have time for:

If day 30 has already passed, catch up before day 60, and failing that, before day 180. Each deadline you beat keeps the next stage from starting.
